text:
As it loses power in Washington, the Trump Administration appears to be doubling down on aggressive immigration enforcement across the country.

What we know:

As it loses power in Washington, the Trump Administration appears to be doubling down on aggressive immigration enforcement across the country.

The architect of the controversial ICE operations was promoted days after sweeping mid-term losses. Immigration attorneys say ICE activity has been ramping back up in Minnesota. And video of an ICE arrest in Robbinsdale last week sparked memories from Operation Metro Surge.

"Thin I.C.E." – a new series from FOX 9 Documentaries– details how immigration operations have escalated during Trump's second term.

"And in each state, it just got worse and worse and worse," said Jose Alvillar, with Unidos Minnesota.

By the time thousands of ICE and Border Patrol agents flooded the Twin Cities metro area last January, a pattern of aggressive tactics and dragnet immigration enforcement had already emerged in other major cities across the country.

From Chicago to Minneapolis

Why you should care:

The Trump Administration has repeatedly claimed they are targeting the "worst of the worst" during immigration operations.

But during Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago last year, they also wrongfully detained immigrants, falsely accused observers of interfering with federal law enforcement and shot at least two people.

The operation in Chicago resulted in numerous legal challenges that revealed federal agents provided misinformation, tampered with evidence and bragged about deadly force.

It foreshadowed what would happen in Minnesota months later.

"I do have very close, very close friends in Minneapolis, one of whom works in immigration, and I did warn them right away, 'they're really coming in hot, they're really coming in aggressive,'" said Theresa Kleinhaus, a civil rights attorney in Chicago.

And yet those warning signs still could not fully prepare Minnesota for the impact of Operation Metro Surge.

More ICE than police

By the numbers:

"Midway Blitz at its height had 500 (agents)," said Gov. Tim Walz. "And we had, by most accounts, I mean, it's hard to get true numbers… above 3,000."

At one point, there were more federal immigration agents in Minneapolis and St. Paul than local police officers.

"In Minneapolis, they could fully saturate and occupy," Kleinhaus said.

The feds deployed four or five times as many agents in a metro area with a much smaller footprint.

"You put 3,000 agents in a very tiny Twin Cities, you’re going to bump into an agent," said Luis Argueta Jr. with Unidos Minnesota.

Unidos Minnesota, which ultimately trained thousands of legal observers, started preparing for a surge in June 2025 after seeing the aggressive tactics being utilized in Los Angeles.

"And so by the time they got to Minnesota, we knew that things were gonna be really bad," Alvillar said.

Operation Metro Surge wound down after the deadly shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti led to widespread criticism of ICE tactics.

After a brief lull, immigration activity has picked up in recent months, according to immigration attorneys.

A 45-year-old man from Mexico who has lived in the country illegally since the late 1990s was recently followed home from the grocery store, punched, and detained in front of his crying daughter.

An attorney for Jose Ruelas Viorato said the detention was unlawful and that Viorato has a Minnesota driver's license, filed the proper immigration paperwork and does not have a violent criminal record.

Adding to the angst that ICE is ramping up aggressive tactics again in Minnesota, Stephen Miller, the architect of the Trump Administration's immigration tactics, was promoted to Chief of Staff days after a blue wave swept the nation's mid-term elections.

DHS defended the arrest and claimed the man threw a bird feeder at agents while trying to flee.

text:
Houston — The siblings of a Mexican construction worker run over last month by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in an unmarked SUV allege the incident that left their brother with severe injuries was "intentional."

"It was not an accident," Miguel Parra Hernandez's sister, Carmen Parra, told CBS News in an exclusive interview. "The videos show everything."

Rodolfo Parra said he cried when he saw videos depicting the Oct. 10 incident that left his brother with a broken leg and hip injuries.

"You can hear all my brother say, 'Ah, you broke my leg. Ah, you're breaking my leg,'" Rodolfo Parra said.

The siblings described 48-year-old Parra Hernandez as a "hardworking" family man who has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, since leaving Mexico in the 1990s as a teenager.

"My brother is not a criminal," Carmen Parra said.

Mario Alberto Morales, the ICE officer who struck Parra Hernandez with his vehicle, was indicted in late October by a Texas grand jury on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Morales' attorney has called the incident an "accident," while ICE has denounced the prosecution as a "political stunt."

"He says he's done"

While Parra Hernandez does not have a criminal history and was not the target of the ICE operation the day he was hit and detained, he remains in the agency's custody, recovering from his injuries. ICE has not disputed that Parra Hernandez lacks a criminal record, but says the Mexican national is in the U.S. illegally and subject to deportation.

Parra Hernandez's siblings claim their brother's mental and physical health has deteriorated while in ICE custody, so much so that he's suffered from suicidal ideation.

"He says he's done," Carmen Parra said. "He wants to just go to sleep and not wake up because he says, 'I'm done in this life.' But we love him."

In a letter to acting ICE Director David Venturella and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday, a group of Democratic lawmakers led by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher accused ICE of obstructing efforts from Parra Hernandez's family and counsel to talk to him and rejecting food brought by relatives.

"The treatment of a long-time community member is unacceptable and a violation of his constitutional rights," the lawmakers said, demanding Parra Hernandez's release.

Representatives for ICE did not respond to questions about Parra Hernandez's health and treatment, and the allegations in the lawmakers' letter.

Parra Hernandez's siblings said he was on his way to work on Oct. 10 when he and a co-worker were approached by ICE agents. Surveillance video shows the two men running out of a white truck and attempting to flee, before an ICE vehicle appears to strike Parra Hernandez from behind.

In a statement following the incident, ICE claims Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle. But Sean Teare, the Harris County district attorney, alleges the ICE agent "aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra Hernandez."

Houston limits cooperation with ICE

Parra Hernandez's hospitalization is one of several ICE-related controversies that Houston Mayor John Whitmire said have spread fear in the Houston area and prompted him to take action.

Following the stunning Republican losses in Texas and across the country on Election Day, Whitmire blocked Houston police officers from contacting ICE when they stop someone who may be in the U.S. without a valid immigration status.

"We do not collaborate unless the person is a really bad person. We're not concerned about someone that got pulled over for a traffic violation, or someone over a noise ordinance," Whitmire told CBS News. "We are going after the bad guys that have committed a new offense, a new danger to our community."

Whitmire said local officials can still work with ICE when someone in the U.S. illegally is booked in jail for criminal conduct.

He argued his executive order is designed to lower "fear and anxiety" in the community, referencing the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant killed by an ICE agent over the summer during an attempted vehicle stop. The deadly shooting remains under investigation.

Since the policy change in Houston, officials in Austin and San Antonio have announced similar proposals.

Whitmire said he's taking a risk with his directive, citing the threat that Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's administration could sue Houston. But Abbott will soon be replaced by Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat to be elected Texas governor in decades, and Whitmire said he can "guarantee" she will not force him to work with ICE.

He also acknowledged the move may prompt the Trump administration to withhold federal funds from Houston.

"Of course, I'm concerned about the Trump administration every day, but you have to use your good judgment," he said.

text:
Protesters at a Contra Costa County courthouse in Martinez rallied against Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who are using a county parking lot to stage operations.

ICE has been using the lot adjacent to the A.F. Bray Courthouse and Martinez Detention Facility, and multiple people have been detained there, said Hernan Soto, an organizer with the Contra Costa Immigrant Rights Alliance, speaking at the protest on Thursday.

“We’re here to let the people and the county know that we know what’s going on,” he said.

ICE’s use of county property is “unacceptable,” he said, but Contra Costa doesn’t prohibit county cooperation with ICE — though immigrant rights activities have called for it for more than a year.

“While other counties are strengthening their policies and issuing cease-and-desist orders to ICE, Contra Costa remains silent,” Soto said.

At a County Board meeting in September, supervisors Shanelle Scales-Preston and John Gioia voted to put forward an ordinance that would require its staff to adhere to rules around interacting with ICE and the agency’s use of county-run facilities.

But Preston and Gioia were outvoted by Candace Andersen, Diane Burgis and Ken Carlson, who opted for a policy — a non-binding guideline — rather than an ordinance, which is a legally binding local law.

The board will vote Tuesday on the proposed policy for responding to Immigration Issues, which is intended to guide county staff on their rights interacting with immigration officers.

In recent weeks, ICE has made itself known in several parts of the county, particularly in an area of Concord known as Monument Corridor, according to Julia Quintero of Monument Impact, a nonprofit organization that serves low-income families.

“The Monument is the holder of most of the immigrant community,” Quintero said at the protest

“We’ve seen a huge increase in the last two weeks,” she said, referring to ICE activity in the neighborhood.

“Monument is a really bustling part of the city, but right now, nobody’s out,” she said. “It automatically puts fear in people’s minds.”

Most of the ICE arrests have targeted men — typically fathers — on their way to work in the morning, Quintero said.

— Griffin Jones, Bay City News

text:
The Trump administration's expanded deportation campaign is delaying home building in New Mexico by creating widespread fear among workers and their families.

Starting in June, arrests of undocumented immigrants and those in the multistep process of becoming U.S.-naturalized citizens have soared to record highs.

Miles Conway, executive vice president and CEO of the New Mexico Home Builders Association, said agents have descended on construction sites, often in unmarked SUVs, to arrest multiple workers.

"The quotes I have heard from my contractors are that job sites are just simply ghost towns. That means at the end of the day, housing prices go up," Conway explained.

An analysis by the New Mexico Office of Housing found the state lacks at least 50,000 affordable housing units for low- and moderate-income households. ICE arrests reached historic highs in the past year, as the second Trump administration narrowed pathways to legal status and expanded the pool of individuals targeted for removal. More than 90,000 arrests were made in June and July, with an additional 50,000 in August.

New Mexico has the highest percentage of Hispanic or Latino residents of any U.S. state. The Trump administration originally said its primary immigration focus would be removing violent criminals, but is now pursuing broader mass deportations, including nonviolent undocumented workers, relying on technical loopholes to evade previous legal limits.

Conway noted one of his largest subcontractors is operating with only 10% of his usual crew and others have reported similar situations. For many in the industry, it is also a human dignity issue.

"A lot of tradespeople absolutely have their documentation in order, and they're being swept up in these administrative warrant raid-like situations. When that happens, that atmosphere of fear really takes hold," Conway observed.

The raids have mostly occurred at large, multifamily developments in New Mexico's largest cities, such as Albuquerque and Santa Fe. Earlier this month, ICE agents arrived in an Albuquerque neighborhood where single-family homes were being built by the global nonprofit Habitat for Humanity.

text:
Hundreds of demonstrators gathered at Rockaway Mall on Saturday to protest plans for a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in neighboring Roxbury.

The demonstration was sparked by a warehouse property in Roxbury that the Department of Homeland Security purchased earlier this year, with plans to convert the site into an ICE detention center.

The project remains tied up in court after a judge issued an order temporarily that prevents DHS from moving forward until an environmental impact study is completed. However, Roxbury Township officials said DHS reportedly signed a contract worth more than $30 million for renovations recently.

"It was a successful delay tactic, but I don't think it was a permanent solution and we have to keep working harder to stop this for good," said Roxbury resident Sierra Winters about the court order.

More than 300 protesters marched through the mall Saturday, voicing concerns about the potential impact the facility could have on immigrant communities across Morris County.

"The Rockaway Mall being so close to Dover, that's the heart of where they're taking our neighbors from," Winters said. "Dover, Hackettstown, Morristown. We've seen ICE raids in all of these local communities and this is where they're going to be planning to bring those folks if this facility is able to be changed into more of a detention center."

Residents also expressed concerns about a potential increased ICE presence in the area with a detention center nearby.

"We're a small community here. We love our neighbors, we love our community and we don't want them to be harassed," said Ronnie Bauman, of Netcong.

Others questioned whether local resources could handle a mass detention facility.

"Water issues, the Highlands Act with the protected land - this would definitely take a toll on our environmental issues as well as, of course, sewage," said Roxbury resident Nicole Maguire.

According to court filings, the Department of Homeland Security, Roxbury Township and the State of New Jersey are required to submit a joint status report to the New Jersey District Court by Tuesday that details actions taken since the court's order was issued in May.

text:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court agreed on Nov. 13 to con­sider the leg­al­ity of Pres­id­ent Don­ald Trump’s restric­tions on access to asylum at the U.S.-Mex­ico bor­der, a hard-line immig­ra­tion policy his admin­is­tra­tion has cred­ited with help­ing reduce bor­der cross­ings.

The justices took up Trump’s appeal of a lower court’s rul­ing that found he exceeded his author­ity by deny­ing migrants caught enter­ing the coun­try illeg­ally the chance to apply for asylum.

The court is expec­ted to hear argu­ments in the case in the com­ing months and rule by the end of June.

Trump, who has described the influx of migrants as an inva­sion, announced the new curbs just hours into his second pres­id­en­tial term on Jan. 20, 2025. His policy sweeps more broadly than sim­ilar curbs put in place by his pre­de­cessor, Joe Biden, who lim­ited asylum eli­gib­il­ity at the south­ern bor­der in a bid to reduce illegal cross­ings.

Trump’s asylum policy is one of a num­ber of meas­ures his admin­is­tra­tion has taken as part of his crack­down on immig­ra­tion pur­sued since return­ing to office last year. Top offi­cials have also sought to per­suade other nations to join in a global cam­paign to roll back asylum pro­tec­tions in an effort to reshape the post-World War II frame­work around human­it­arian migra­tion.

Under Trump’s policy, migrants caught cross­ing the south­ern bor­der illeg­ally are barred from pur­su­ing asylum claims. The pro­hib­i­tion also applies to migrants who arrive at offi­cial bor­der cross­ings and lack cer­tain med­ical or crim­inal his­tory inform­a­tion, a require­ment that advoc­ates say is often impossible to meet for people flee­ing viol­ence.

Trump’s pro­clam­a­tion announ­cing the asylum restric­tions – and the fasttrack deport­a­tion pro­ced­ures they are meant to enable – said the policy would remain in effect until the Repub­lican pres­id­ent determ­ines that the “inva­sion at the south­ern bor­der” has ended.

Immig­rant rights groups filed a class-action law­suit chal­len­ging the policy on behalf of would-be asylum­seekers who say they were denied a “cred­ible fear” inter­view by U.S. immig­ra­tion offi­cials before facing deport­a­tion. Such inter­views are meant to determ­ine whether migrants seek­ing asylum would face per­se­cu­tion in their home coun­try based on race, reli­gion, nation­al­ity, mem­ber­ship in a par­tic­u­lar social group or polit­ical opin­ion.

A fed­eral judge in Wash­ing­ton, DC, ruled in favor of the immig­rant rights groups in July 2025. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Dis­trict of Columbia Cir­cuit in April upheld the judge’s rul­ing but largely agreed to block the decision from tak­ing effect to let the admin­is­tra­tion appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 con­ser­vat­ive major­ity, has been largely defer­en­tial to Trump in his second pres­id­en­tial term in chal­lenges to his immig­ra­tion policies.

In June, the court handed Trump a vic­tory by back­ing the fed­eral gov­ern­ment’s author­ity to turn away asylum­seekers when offi­cials deem U.S.-Mex­ico bor­der cross­ings too over­burdened to handle addi­tional claims.

In Septem­ber, the court let the admin­is­tra­tion resume deport­ing migrants to coun­tries other than their own without offer­ing them the chance to show the harms they may face. The justices are due to hear argu­ments over the leg­al­ity of that policy on Dec. 9.

The Week Ahead: The Article III branch of government is doing its job. The Article I branch will be back in business come January. And the voters have spoken. Everyone seemed to understand the shift in the country—except for Trump and those closest to him—as we started the new week.

Not With a Bang, but a Whimper: Officials Leave the Justice Department: We looked into the resignations of four senior DOJ officials, all heading for the exits after barely a year and a half on the job. This is the sort of turnover that raises a serious question: What’s going on inside the Justice Department? (Spoiler alert: it’s Todd Blanche.)

Live with Katie Phang: Katie and I discussed what we’re still celebrating from last week’s election, how we analyze developing legal issues this week, and what we think the work ahead of us is going to look like, if we want to take back our country.

A Failed Impeachment, for Now: Congressman Dan Goldman Explains what happened: Congressman Dan Goldman, who served as the lead counsel for the House Intelligence Committee investigation that led to Donald Trump’s first impeachment, joined us Tuesday to explain the failed impeachment of Pete Hegseth. It’s a must-watch if you missed it earlier this week.

New Information About ICE with Katie Benner: NYT reporter Katie Benner joined us Wednesday morning to discuss her new reporting, which is headlined, “ICE Officer Involved in Maine Shooting Expressed Anti-Immigrant Hatred.” She discussed evidence of motive and read an email sent several years earlier to a family member by the ICE agent who shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero. If you’re outraged by how the Trump administration has deployed ICE and ignored the use of force against people on American streets, this case will be especially interesting to you, because, as Katie explains, accountability is a possibility here.

Essay Five in the Republic Revisited Series: Why Democracy Is Still Worth It: We’ve spent a lot of time discussing how democracies die. But Wednesday, we turned to a question that matters even more: Why ours is worth fighting for and saving. We discussed what makes it so valuable, and how we explain that to people who aren’t convinced—or who simply haven’t thought much about what they stand to lose. The excerpt from my book, Giving Up Is Unforgivable, is about more than understanding threats to democracy. It’s about finding the words, the ideas, and the conviction to explain why it matters. If you missed Wednesday’s discussion, I hope you’ll read it. If you’re doing your holiday shopping, a little shameless self-promotion: the book makes a great gift for people who are newly paying attention after the elections.

It’s Official in Mississippi: When Scott Colom spoke to a full house as Mississippi’s newest senator, everyone was listening, including people in Georgia, where similar progress has been made, and Alabama and Louisiana, which have fallen short but where fresh inspiration from Colom’s win is already being put into action for future elections. We looked at Colom’s historic win and what it suggests for future elections and our democracy.

Five Questions with Mississippi Voting Rights Lawyer Amir Badat: When early election results showed the Democrat in the Mississippi Senate race, Scott Colom, ahead by just a few hundred votes, Amir Badat did not have to get on a plane or hop in a car to get to Mississippi. That’s because Amir lives there. He’s a voting rights expert who understands the ins and outs of Mississippi’s electoral system, voting laws, and local politics. In this Five Questions interview, he helps us understand Mississippi's vote count, including how the secretary of state’s insistence on using Experian data made it more difficult for some Mississippians to vote.

Stephen Miller’s Selective American Dream: Back in 2018, Stephen Miller’s uncle wrote a piece speaking to the hypocrisy of his nephew’s support for anti-immigrant policies, despite their family's immigrant story. We revisit that criticism of Miller in light of his new role as Trump’s chief of staff.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested and deported more people during the last fiscal year than at any time in its 23-year history, Homeland Security said Thursday, as President Donald Trump followed through on promises of mass deportations that helped him win back the White House in 2024 but also fueled the political blowback that led to Democrats’ overwhelming victory in last week’s midterm elections.

The numbers released Thursday by the department reflect the massive funding that has gone into supercharging immigration enforcement under the Trump administration, with more money for deportation officers, detention facilities and deportation flights.

But Democratic members of Congress, buoyed by their sweeping victories in both the House and Senate, are promising vigorous oversight of the agency core to the president's mass deportation mission.

ICE said it deported 483,200 people in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30. In 2014, 405,090 people were deported under then-President Barack Obama, when some activists labeled him the “deporter in chief.”

The 2026 number was up 9% from its previous high of 442,640 in the same period a year earlier and up 78% from 271,480 in 2024, the last year of Joe Biden's presidency.

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Details of ICE arrests remain fuzzy

Yet much remained unsaid in the DHS press release, including how many deportees had criminal histories and a detailed breakdown of the statistics. In addition, deportation numbers can be notoriously fuzzy, with totals counted in different ways in different years. And the Trump administration largely stopped publishing regular data on immigration enforcement once it took office, instead releasing information intermittently in press releases or on social media without the detailed data reports that it used to deliver.

“It is accurate that ICE is making record numbers of arrests,” said Marc R. Rosenblum, a visiting fellow at the Migration Policy Institute and a former top official overseeing statistics at the Department of Homeland Security. “They have record resources. They've doubled their staffing. They’re getting a lot of support from other law enforcement agencies.”

But the sparse data in Thursday's announcement means “we can't really see what’s going on in any kind of detailed way.”

Homeland Security's statistics office used to publish data monthly about immigration arrests and deportations, while ICE's website used to have a dashboard detailing information about ICE detentions, arrests and deportations. But that stopped at the beginning of the second Trump administration, raising questions about how many people the department was actually arresting and removing from the country.

The conservative Oversight Project, which would like to see the administration carry out more deportations, has filed a lawsuit seeking to get deportation data from the government.

Scott Mechowski is a visiting fellow for deportation studies at the Oversight Project and used to be ICE’s deputy field office director for enforcement and removal operations in New York. He said without more detailed information from the department about how they're counting deportations and what they're including, he's skeptical of the figures released Thursday.

“Show me the data," said Mechowski. “Even if the numbers are what they said they were, even then, it’s going to fall short of the president’s campaign promise.”

The Oversight Project has released a report detailing how the administration can reached the promised million deportations a year, including by ramping up arrests and enforcement at worksites.

Many voters found Trump's deportation efforts excessive

Trump had campaigned on ridding America of criminal migrants, saying he’d be targeting the “worst of the worst.”

But that is rarely the case. In July, for instance, only roughly one-quarter of deportees had criminal convictions, according to the Deportation Data Project. More than half weren't even facing charges.

The numbers released Thursday also fell well short of the White House goal of 1 million deportations annually, a promise it made when it received billions in additional funding from Congress, supercharging the government's immigration bureaucracy.

Trump returned to power last year promising to end illegal crossings at the southern border. His administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and speeded up deportations. Immigration crackdown operations are often purposefully high-profile, in part to frighten migrants into leaving of their own accord.

But the crackdown hasn't always gone as planned.

The biggest shift came earlier this year in Minneapolis, when more than 2,000 federal officers were deployed to the city and thousands of protesters turned out to confront masked and often heavily armed agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles.

Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 — were killed in confrontations with officers, and the administration quickly backed away from high-profile operations.

While arrests dropped after the killings, they quickly returned to record numbers, albeit in quieter immigration sweeps.

By last week's elections the White House's immigration message had splintered, with even some deeply Republican rural areas voting Democratic after people saw longtime migrant neighbors, many of them key workers on farms, ranches and meat processing facilities, taken in arrests.

The highest recorded number of deportations on record came during President Dwight D. Eisenhower’s crackdown on illegal immigrants from Mexico. The often-chaotic policy saw deportation numbers spike dramatically in the early 1950s, cresting at 1.1 million in 1954.

description:
The Department of Justice has officially signaled a major shift in how it handles immigration detention lawsuits in the Western District of Washington.
This move comes as the office struggles to keep up with a massive surge in habeas corpus petitions that have flooded the district dockets since the summer.
The Department of Justice claims that the current workload has negatively impacted its ability to handle other civil litigation cases.
The department also reserves the right to jump back into a case if it determines that its involvement is necessary.
This change is expected to significantly streamline and expedite the resolution of most habeas petitions, providing more discretion to the District Court.
text:
The Department of Justice has officially signaled a major shift in how it handles immigration detention lawsuits in the Western District of Washington. Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd sent a letter in late October to Chief U.S. District Judge David S. Estudillo, stating that the government will stop defending Immigration and Customs Enforcement in a large portion of these courtroom battles, as per Law and Crime‘s report.

This move comes as the office struggles to keep up with a massive surge in habeas corpus petitions that have flooded the district dockets since the summer. The court previously put a specialized process in place to help speed up how these cases are handled, and while the Department of Justice admits this has helped with uniformity, it has also led to a continuous increase in the number of petitions. According to the letter, the government is dealing with dozens of these filings every single week.

The Department of Justice claims that the current workload has negatively impacted its ability to handle other civil litigation cases. Attorneys are spending a significant amount of time on these immigration matters, including preparing status reports, supplemental briefing, and fighting motions related to the Equal Access to Justice Act. The letter notes that the office is also frequently responding to orders from the court that stem from technical violations of the scheduling process.

Because of these resource constraints, the office says it can no longer guarantee legal representation for ICE or its agents

The letter is quite blunt about the situation, stating, “The [U.S. Attorney’s Office] unfortunately does not have the available resources, at this juncture, to continue entering [DOJ] appearances in every one of the dozens of §2241 Immigration Petitions filed each week.”

There are a few important details to keep in mind regarding how this will actually play out in court. The Department of Justice is not completely walking away from the table. The office intends to keep reviewing new petitions and scheduling orders as they arrive. They will also keep sending those orders to the relevant contacts at ICE. The department also reserves the right to jump back into a case if it determines that its involvement is necessary.

However, the new process sets a very specific timeline for the court to follow. If the Department of Justice does not file a notice of appearance within seven court days, the court can move forward and rule on the merits of the petition without the government providing a defense. This means the government will not be responsible for helping move the case along or serving as a middleman between the court and the respondents.

This change is expected to significantly streamline and expedite the resolution of most habeas petitions, providing more discretion to the District Court. The decision currently impacts the Western District of Washington, an area that covers more than 6 million people and includes cities like Tacoma and Olympia.

text:
Anti-ICE campaigners on social media have scored a big win with a recent legal ruling

A new court order will prohibit government officials from censoring Mark Hodges and Kae Rosado, both Midwesterners who ran platforms where users could share their videos of ICE activity, with the aim of documenting excessive use of force or abuses of power.

Mark Hodges created "Eyes Up", an app for sharing videos of ICE operations, while Rosado ran a Facebook group called "ICE Sightings – Chicagoland." Eyes Up was removed from the App Store by Apple in October 2025, while the Facebook group was removed by Meta in October 2025.

The news follows a lawsuit kicked off by the non-profit Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) in February. The suit accused then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem of infringing on the pair's First Amendment rights, by "coercing" the social media platforms to remove the group and mobile app.

The ruling makes permanent a preliminary injunction granted by District Judge Jorge Alonso in April, which states that the government officials "shall take no actions, formal or informal, to demand or pressure" Facebook and Apple to suppress or continue to suppress either the group or the app.

In earlier court proceedings, Alonso found that although Bondi and Noem's statements may not have constituted direct threats to prosecute Facebook and Apple, they were "intimations of a threat." He added that "thinly veiled threats such as these constitute sufficient evidence on which Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claim."

FIRE Senior Attorney Colin McDonell commented on the recent decision: "This is not a partisan issue, and FIRE is here to challenge any government actors who would seek to stifle our freedom of speech."

He added that the First Amendment "protects our right to share truthful information about our government and its activities."

text:
More than 70 protestors gathered for a prayer vigil and rally Saturday in Appleton after Immigration and Customs Enforcement began transporting detainees to the newly opened facility.

The protesters gathered to hold signs, sing and chant, asking for more transparency and expressing frustration at the immigration policies of the federal government. They also called for humane conditions, including access to food, clean water and communication with their families and attorneys.

Brian Wojtalewicz, an attorney in Appleton, said during a press conference before the rally they believe more than 70 detainees are being held in the facility. The Sahan Journal has reported the facility has up to 1,600 beds.

“We are not alone at being appalled that human beings have been imprisoned out here,” Wojtalewicz said. “What are their sins? Their sins are traveling thousands of miles to get better jobs, to get safe communities, to have their children live in safety, have their children get a decent education. That's their sins.”

Yolanda Cisneros, a member of Unidos MN in Granite Falls, said previous actions of Republican President Donald Trump’s administration and ICE require transparency due to lack of trust.

“There are still many questions that deserve answers," Cisneros said. "How many more are expected to come? What are the conditions like inside the facility? How are the detainees being treated? And what procedures are in place to ensure their safety and well being? These are not unreasonable questions."

Clergy and citizens, like Pastor Andrés Albertsen, also voiced concern for immigrant neighbors, not only inside the detention facility, but among their communities.

"The opening of this facility sends a painful message," Albersten said. "The policies that caused so much fear have not changed, and they continue to live with that fear. That fear has a human cost."

Observers noticed the facility, formerly owned by CoreCivic and vacant since 2010, began seeing higher levels of activity on Wednesday. The Department of Homeland Security stated in a release that the Appleton Detention Facility opened Nov. 9.

The former private prison has been controversial since ICE purchased the facility in August. KARE 11 reported the prison, which was for sale for $75 million, was purchased by the Trump administration for $495.6 million.

MPR News has requested a response from Homeland Security officials, which has not yet responded.

This is the third major immigration-related case the high court has agreed to hear this term.
The justices also will decide whether the Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries to which they have no ties to and whether immigrants can be indefinitely detained.

text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to decide whether the federal government can ban asylum claims at the southern border.

One of President Donald Trump’s first proclamations he signed at the start of his second term was a ban on asylum claims at the southern border on the grounds that there was an “invasion,” which the administration argued was a condition that allowed the president to invoke a section of the law to suspend asylum claims.

A federal judge found the policy unlawful, but decided to allow it to remain while litigation is pursued. An appeals court upheld the lower court’s decision.

The justices agreed to answer two questions, whether the proclamation that bans asylum is lawful and if a class action suit should be allowed. The case will be argued sometime during the coming months.

This is the third major immigration-related case the high court has agreed to hear this term. The justices also will decide whether the Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries to which they have no ties to and whether immigrants can be indefinitely detained.

The justices earlier this year allowed the Trump administration to use a policy known as “metering” which allows immigration officials to turn away migrants applying from asylum at the southern border.

The American Civil Liberties Union is representing the three immigration groups that brought the suit: the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, the Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project.

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

A decision from the justices is likely next summer.

text:
Activists fear Bangkok will give in to pressure from Beijing despite reports of torture and human rights abuses against the mostly Muslim ethnic minority

The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.

Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN. The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.

Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.

The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.

Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.

Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.

The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.

Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.

Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.

Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.

In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.

The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.

Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.

It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.

Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.

Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.

A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”

A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.

description:
Not Marin County.
Thousands of Marin residents have spoken, written and petitioned the supervisors to end county cooperation with ICE and to pass an “ICE-free” law.
Restricting ICE in public spaces is precisely what “ICE-free” laws like Assembly Bill 1807 does for state property, and county “ICE-free” ordinances do for county property.
What would a Marin “ICE-free” law do?
Pass an “ICE-free” law.
text:
Marin County leaders took no formal action to restrict local activities by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agency during President Donald Trump’s first term. Twenty-two months into his second term, our Board of Supervisors has not agendized or discussed the sanctuary protections that have been adopted by 48 of California’s 58 counties.

It passed a resolution condemning racism and supporting democracy, and has provided funding for immigrant services, but has imposed no concrete restrictions on ICE activity.

Many watched in horror as ICE took over the streets of Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis, commandeering parks, parking lots and other public property for brutal, military-style operations. The actions led cities and counties to pass “ICE-free” laws barring the agency from using their property, resources, data and personnel for immigration enforcement without a judicial warrant. Not Marin County.

With no law to stop them, ICE agents continue to stage and carry out detentions in the parking lots and public lobby of the Marin Civic Center and the county jail. Marin County Sheriff Scardina, who has no legal obligation to do so, publishes booking logs to assist ICE. He appears to be honoring what are unenforceable administrative warrants by ICE. According to the Marin Rapid Response Network, at least a quarter of all ICE detentions of Marin County residents since March 2025 have happened on county property – all seemingly with information or assistance from the Sheriff’s Office.

Thousands of Marin residents have spoken, written and petitioned the supervisors to end county cooperation with ICE and to pass an “ICE-free” law. Instead, after a year of inaction, the county has run what I consider a misleading PR campaign, passing off a state-mandated internal policy as the equivalent of a law.

All California counties are required, under Senate Bill 580, to adopt a policy by Jan. 1 to guide their staff when dealing with ICE. That law makes it clear that the policies impose no legal restrictions on ICE.

Enforceable prohibitions require a law. But with the SB 580 deadline looming, county officials appear to have seized the PR opportunity. They presented the policy with much fanfare at the Oct. 20 Board of Supervisors meeting – including comments from six different county representatives – and published social-media posts claiming the new policy prohibits ICE staging and enforcement activity on county property. I think they are wrong.

Restricting ICE in public spaces is precisely what “ICE-free” laws like Assembly Bill 1807 does for state property, and county “ICE-free” ordinances do for county property. That’s why AB 1807 and similar laws include provisions for the development and posting of signs on government-owned public property prohibiting ICE enforcement on the premises.

What would a Marin “ICE-free” law do? Modeled on AB 1807, it would prohibit ICE enforcement activity — including parking, gathering and staging — on all public and private areas of county property. Marin officials would post signs on county property prohibiting ICE enforcement on the premises; the Sheriff’s Office would notify ICE of the law’s prohibitions; and front-line staff would have handouts to share if approached by ICE agents describing the law and its penalties that could include both civil and criminal liability. If agents ignored county signs and directives, the law would be enforceable in court. And a law could end the Sheriff’s Office voluntary cooperation with ICE.

On Nov. 10, supervisors acted with urgency and used that power to approve a moratorium on the construction of ICE detention centers. While the agency has not undertaken or proposed to construct such a facility in Marin, it is good to be proactive. But why has the Board of Supervisors failed to act with the same urgency to end the escalating ICE activity taking place right under their noses at the Civic Center?

The federal government’s $250 billion war seemingly targeting immigrants of color is just getting started. ICE recently launched a 45-day surge in California leading to an uptick in Marin. An “ICE-free” law won’t keep agents out of Marin altogether, but it will sharply limit where and how ICE operates here.

Only an “ICE-free” law will bar the escalating activity at the Marin Civic Center and other county properties. Only the supervisors have the power to make this happen. Facing a growing humanitarian crisis, the board must use the strongest tools it has to protect our immigrant neighbors. Pass an “ICE-free” law.

Tammy Edmonson is a co-founder of Mill Valley Force for Racial Equity and Empowerment. Learn more at mvfree.org.

text:
The governments of Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Greece plan to announce on Monday, November 16, at a meeting in Vienna, the creation in Central Africa of the first center outside the European Union for foreigners who have been denied asylum.

Politico reported that five European nations have finalized an agreement to send migrants to a dedicated deportation hub in Rwanda, citing three sources familiar with the negotiations.

According to information from the InfoMigrants portal, at the initial stage, it will be a pilot project designed for about 100 people—each of the five participating countries will send around 20 migrants to Kigali.

The center is expected to become operational in 2027, although it remains unknown whether the Hope Hostel complex, previously paid for by the United Kingdom, will be used for this purpose.

The authors of the initiative emphasize the key difference between their model and the British one:

they intend to deport to Rwanda not those foreigners whose asylum applications are still pending, but only those who have already received a final rejection, exhausted all legal appeals in Europe, and are required to leave the territory of the European Union.

They will stay at the African center until European authorities organize their departure to their countries of origin.

How EU laws were changed and what role Frontex will receive

The current agreement was made possible thanks to a large-scale revision of EU migration rules. As Deutsche Welle explains, European courts previously regularly blocked attempts to deport migrants to third countries if the individual had no personal connection to that state—such as relatives, language proficiency, or prior residence.

However, on October 16, 2026, the new EU Return Regulation came into force, replacing the 2008 directive and abolishing the requirement for a prior connection to the country of destination if an interstate agreement exists.

The new document also introduced a single European return order: a deportation decision issued by one member state now automatically applies in all others without a review of the case.

In addition, the regulation explicitly permitted the establishment of "return hubs" outside the EU, with the exception of accommodating unaccompanied minors there.

Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris clarified in an interview with ANT1 television that the center is planned to launch in the second half of 2027—just when Athens takes over the presidency of the Council of the EU. According to the minister, these will not be closed prisons, but "open facilities." To avoid human rights lawsuits, the five European countries will independently fund the project and formally retain legal responsibility for the transferred individuals, while planning to involve UN bodies and the International Organization for Migration in monitoring.

Concurrently, the European Commission proposed expanding the powers of the border agency Frontex by establishing a Return Coordination Center within it. If the reform is approved, the agency will be able to organize deportation flights not only from Europe, but also directly from one third country to another—for example, from a hub in Rwanda to the migrant's homeland.

Four volunteers for 966 million dollars: the experience of predecessors

As The New York Times notes, all previous attempts by Western governments to offshore migration procedures ended in legal blocks and multimillion-dollar losses.

The most telling was the British project of 2022–2024, initiated by the Conservative cabinets of Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak. London planned to forcibly send illegal migrants who crossed the English Channel to Rwanda so their applications could be processed in Africa. In 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled the scheme unlawful due to a real risk that Kigali would deport asylum seekers back to countries where their lives would be in danger.

By the time Keir Starmer's Labour government permanently scrapped the program in 2024, British taxpayers had spent £715 million on it—around €835 million, or $966 million. Over the entire duration, only four people left for Rwanda under this scheme, and they did so voluntarily in exchange for a financial payment.

Italy faced similar difficulties when, in 2024 under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, it built two centers in Albania for the expedited processing of migrants intercepted in the Mediterranean. Italian courts immediately blocked this practice, ruling that countries of origin such as Egypt or Bangladesh cannot automatically be deemed safe for all categories of citizens.

As a result, starting in March 2025, Rome repurposed one of the Albanian centers in the town of Gjadër exclusively as a detention facility for men who had already been refused asylum in Italy. Over the course of a year and a half, only about 500 people passed through it, whereas the total cost of the Albanian project through 2028 is estimated at over €670 million, or $775 million.

Denmark also has its own experience: in 2021, Copenhagen passed a law on deporting asylum seekers outside Europe and signed a memorandum with Rwanda, but froze negotiations in early 2023 under pressure from the European Commission, subsequently deciding to act within a coalition with other EU countries. Even earlier, between 2013 and 2018, Israel sent thousands of natives of Eritrea and Sudan to Rwanda and Uganda under covert agreements, until the program was partially halted by the Israeli Supreme Court following reports from human rights advocates that deported individuals remained in Africa without legal status or documentation.

"Migration diplomacy" of Paul Kagame

Despite the modest scale of the pilot project, the governments of the five countries view it as the beginning of a broader system. Danish Migration Minister Morten Bødskov stated that Europe "simply needs a way to quickly expel people who have no legal grounds to stay here." And in the coalition agreement of the new Dutch government signed in January 2026, the ultimate goal was explicitly stated as the complete offshoring of the submission and processing of asylum applications outside Europe, so that no such procedure is ever conducted on Dutch territory again.

Within the European Union itself, this approach sparks controversy. Spain and France have previously opposed offshoring migration centers. French President Emmanuel Macron expressed skepticism toward such initiatives this year: "I have never seen a return center in a third country that actually worked." Alberto-Horst Neidhardt, head of the migration programme at the European Policy Centre think tank, believes that deporting several dozen or hundred people will not solve the problem, but serves politicians as an instrument of "political signaling" to voters amid the rising popularity of far-right parties.

Human rights organizations, in turn, warn of the legal vacuum in which deported people risk finding themselves if their countries of origin refuse to take them back.

In a statement by the organization, Eve Geddie, Director of Amnesty International's European Institutions Office, called the prospective centers "cruel human rights black holes."

Sjoerd Warmerdam, head of the Dutch refugee assistance organization VluchtelingenWerk, noted that even the Dutch immigration service itself does not consider Rwanda a safe third country, and that independent monitoring there is "virtually impossible."

Clémentine de Montjoye, Africa researcher at Human Rights Watch, recalled the brutal suppression of dissent in Rwanda, while Dutch MEP Anna Strolenberg, who recently visited Kigali, pointed out that local authorities are willing to accept any proposals from Europeans without adequate security guarantees.

Experts also point to the geopolitical price of the agreement. According to Toni Haastrup, professor of global politics at the University of Manchester, for Rwandan President Paul Kagame, such deals with the West and the US are a means of bolstering international status and a lever of influence over the European Union.

As early as September 2025, the European Parliament urged the European Commission to review financial aid to Rwandan state institutions due to torture, arbitrary detentions, and military support for the M23 rebel group in the neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo. However, the reliance of European governments on migration cooperation with Kigali, analysts note, will make any criticism directed at the Rwandan authorities significantly more difficult.

text:
When the next Congress convenes in January, Democrats will hold large majorities on Capitol Hill—likely 56 seats in the Senate and about 260 in the House of Representatives. For Donald Trump, the numbers seem to pose an existential question: Exactly how many of those lawmakers will he try to put in jail?

If the administration’s recent online posting is any indication, that figure could be very high indeed.

Let’s start with the president himself. “Will the Seditious Six ever be prosecuted?” he demanded on Truth Social last week. “What they did was a great violation to our Country and its Constitution!” That’s a reference to Democratic Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly, and Reps. Jason Crow, Chris Deluzio, Maggie Goodlander, and Chrissy Houlahan, who last year released a viral video encouraging members of the military and intelligence community to refuse to carry out illegal orders.

The video enraged Trump, who suggested the lawmakers were “traitors” who should be executed. Despite the fact that the video was quite obviously constitutionally protected speech, the Justice Department in February reportedly tried to convince a grand jury to indict those member of Congress—an effort that failed spectacularly. Now, Trump appears to want his DOJ to try again.

The administration is also threatening criminal charges against members of Congress if they use their oversight authority in ways the White House deems improper. As Politico put it, “Trump wants Democrats investigating him to be afraid. Very afraid.”

In a November 9 letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, White House Counsel William Scharf warned, “We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government.” Scharf added such congressional efforts “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

Aaron Reitz, Trump’s US Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, has also been firing off letters. In the past five days, he has implied he could file criminal charges against Sen. Richard Blumenthal in response to Blumenthal’s investigation of White House ballroom donors; against Slotkin over comments she recently made about investigating Trump staffers; and against Sen. Elizabeth Warren over how she plans to conduct investigations as chair of the Senate Banking Committee.

Other current and incoming Democratic members of Congress that Trump’s team has sought to prosecute include: Brad Lander (acquitted on charges of obstructing immigration agents), Sen. Adam Schiff (no charges filed over mortgage fraud allegations), and Rep. Lamonica McIver (currently facing charges for supposedly assaulting or interfering with federal officers during an immigration protest). And in October, Department of Homeland Security agents raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar—a longtime target of Trump.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline travel this weekend, using the incident to push Congress on money to fully upgrade America’s air traffic control system.

The Republican president has been conspicuously quiet on the ground stop since it began Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.

Trump said in a new post on his social media platform that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in “drips and drabs.” The Republican-controlled Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Federal Aviation Administration as part of the party’s sweeping tax cut package last year, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly characterized that funding as a down payment on a broader overhaul of the aging system.

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trump wrote on social media Sunday. “It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!”

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing Joe Biden’s administration of making an “old and broken system worse than when they began.”

Biden signed a massive infrastructure bill into law in the first year of his presidency, which set aside $25 billion for the FAA to improve airports and its traffic control towers, to redevelop airport terminals, to “upgrade the foundation” of the air traffic control system, according to the FAA.

Duffy was the administration’s public face on the ground stop across the Sunday news shows, pressing Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air traffic control infrastructure.

In a post on the social media platform X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. had secured two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting “deep diagnostics” on the equipment. He has said the problem began when L3Harris was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload.

After the wire was replaced at the site in El Dorado, Ark., and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, cascading into the ground stop. “We didn’t think that should or would happen, he told ABC’s “This Week.”

As for the traveling public, he told CBS’ “Face the Nation” that “we have some delays in the airspace right now,” but looking to the end of the day and into Monday, “we should be running at full capacity.”

In a ground stop, airplanes and crews are taken out of position, he said, “so it takes a little bit of time for the airliners to get back … at full capacity and operation but we’re well on our way.”

text:
CPJ Urges US to Release Afghan Journalist Facing Deportation to Taliban-Controlled Afghanistan

—————————————–

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) has called on US immigration authorities to immediately release Afghan journalist Shaban Ali Rafat and grant him a full hearing on his asylum case, warning that deportation to Afghanistan could expose him to persecution and torture under Taliban rule.

In a statement issued on November 13, 2026, CPJ said Rafat had been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in California since January 21, 2025. His lawyer, David Tarr, warned that he now faces deportation despite previous findings indicating a serious risk of torture if returned to Afghanistan.

Before the Taliban takeover in August 2021, Rafat worked as a reporter and producer for state-owned Maaref TV and as a senior media officer at Kabul University. His reporting included the November 2020 university attack and the persecution of Afghanistan’s Hazara community.

On November 6, a US magistrate judge recommended granting Rafat’s habeas corpus petition and releasing him under supervision, ruling that his continued detention was unreasonable. The recommendation remains subject to review by a district judge.

CPJ also highlighted growing restrictions on media serving Afghanistan’s Hazara and Shia communities. In 2026, Taliban authorities shut down Tamadon TV, Rah-e-Farda TV and the Afghan Voice Agency, while detaining journalists and senior media personnel associated with the outlets.

The organisation warned that returning Rafat to Afghanistan would place him at risk because of his journalistic work and urged US authorities to respect press freedom and human rights protections.

title: Can we trust Trump on immigration reform, even 'un poquito?' - Local News Pasadena
description:
His announcement was not accompanied by a legislative proposal or even the general outlines of a possible immigration reform plan.
Immigration reform without clearly identified beneficiaries, without a legislative proposal, and without verifiable commitments is not reform.
Therefore, any presidential statement favoring immigration reform must also be examined in light of the power retained by those who have designed and defended these policies.
But it would be a serious mistake to interpret this new political environment as a guarantee of immigration reform.
Because when it comes to Donald Trump’s promises on immigration reform, we cannot afford to trust him, not even a little, ‘ni un poquito.’
text:
On November 8, 2026, CBS aired an exclusive interview with President Donald Trump on its program 60 Minutes that left supporters and critics alike astonished, including me.

During the taped conversation, the president said he was willing to work with Democrats to address major national problems. When interviewer Ross Douthat asked him to identify a specific issue he would be willing to tackle through cooperation with the new Democratic majority in Congress, Trump’s answer was as unexpected as it was surprising: immigration.

Yes, immigration.

The very issue he has used for years as an instrument of political confrontation and as justification for an aggressive campaign of arrests and deportations against ‘nuestras familias.’ He said that his deportation policy “might be too tough.” The unavoidable question is: How much credibility should we give Donald Trump when he talks about immigration reform? We know his credibility fluctuates more than crypto coins’ value or Tesla’s stock market price.

Those of us who have fought for more than four decades for fair, comprehensive, and generous immigration reform cannot afford to confuse a presidential statement with a genuine political commitment. Especially when the future and stability of millions of undocumented workers and their families are at stake, to understand and place in context the president’s possible true intentions, let us examine some of the most revealing episodes in his political record over the past ten years.

Broken campaign promises – ‘Unas promesas de campaña incumplidas’

During his first term, in 2017, Trump expressed willingness to work with Democrats to resolve the plight of the so-called Dreamers permanently: young immigrants brought to the United States by their parents when they were still children. In 2012, President Barack Obama had established the DACA program, granting these young people temporary protection from deportation and renewable work permits. Trump promised to negotiate a permanent solution. However, the negotiations failed, and his administration ultimately pursued measures to eliminate the DACA program. Trump’s first major immigration promise became yet another missed opportunity.

Years later, in April 2026, the president again expressed his willingness to address the concerns of farmers who were reporting labor shortages resulting from the immigration raids and deportations carried out by his administration. In June 2025, he expanded his statements to include workers in hotels, restaurants and other service industries. He appeared to be finally acknowledging an undeniable economic reality: millions of immigrant workers, including undocumented immigrants, are indispensable to the operation of major sectors of the American economy.

I would call it ‘hipocresía.’

But once again, his words failed to produce concrete legislative proposals. Within days, on June 17, the Department of Homeland Security told agents to resume raids at farms, hotels and restaurants. While speaking of solutions, his administration continued conducting immigration arrests and deportation operations in cities across the country. In Los Angeles, these actions generated fear, outrage, and profound uncertainty among thousands of immigrant families. The contradiction was unmistakable: while acknowledging the economic necessity of these workers, his government continued to arrest and deport them.

More than a contradiction, I would call it ‘hipocresía.’

Another promise without concrete commitment – ‘Otra promesa sin ompromiso concreto‘

My initial reaction to Trump’s statements on 60 Minutes was one of extreme caution. And there are compelling reasons for that caution. His announcement was not accompanied by a legislative proposal or even the general outlines of a possible immigration reform plan. Nor did he identify the Republican lawmakers who would be responsible for drafting such legislation or the Democratic leaders with whom he intended to negotiate. ‘Nadie, ninguno, anónimos’.

More importantly, he failed to explain what kind of immigration protection he would be willing to grant to millions of undocumented workers who have lived and worked in the United States for years, even decades. Would he support a permanent residency program? Would he offer only temporary work permits? Would he consider a pathway to American citizenship? Who would benefit? Agricultural workers? Service industry employees? Parents of U.S. citizen children? None of these questions were answered. ‘Como siempre dando atole con el dedo’.

Immigration reform without clearly identified beneficiaries, without a legislative proposal, and without verifiable commitments is not reform. It’s a mirage in the desert. At best, it is a statement of intentions. If the president genuinely intended to rebuild trust, he could accompany his words with concrete actions. For example, he could order a review of immigration enforcement priorities to protect undocumented workers with many years of residence, strong family ties, and no criminal records. He did not say he would do so.

Nor did he explain how he would confront the most hardline elements of the Republican Party, which have historically opposed virtually every proposal for broad immigration legalization.

It is not enough to promise immigration reform. A president must demonstrate a willingness to confront those who oppose it, even within his own political party, as President Ronald Reagan did in 1986, signing the Immigration Reform and Control Act into law on November 6, 1986—exactly a few days over 40 years ago this month.

However, this time Democrats hold majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The ogre of Santa Monica: Stephen Miller – El ogro de Santa Mónica: Stephen Miller

Another fundamental consideration is Stephen Miller. Recently appointed White House Chief of Staff, Miller has been one of the principal architects of Donald Trump’s most restrictive immigration policies for years. His influence within the White House is hardly a minor detail. It is a decisive factor in understanding the direction of presidential immigration policy. Since Trump’s first term, Miller has promoted immigration restrictions, expanded deportation policies, and measures intended to limit opportunities for immigration protection. This native Californian is the brain behind the ICE persecution of many truly native Californios.

Therefore, any presidential statement favoring immigration reform must also be examined in light of the power retained by those who have designed and defended these policies. The problem is not simply what Trump says in front of television cameras. The problem is what his administration does every single day. While he speaks of possible agreements with Democrats, thousands of immigrant families continue facing arrests, prolonged detention, and deportations that separate parents from their U.S. citizen children.

That reality does not disappear because of a presidential statement. ‘Puro bla, bla, bla...’

And as long as Stephen Miller continues to exercise decisive influence over immigration policy, there are compelling reasons to demand concrete action before granting credibility to new promises. A government’s true intentions are measured by its actions, not by the words of its president, scripted by the ogre advising him on immigration.

The response of immigrant workers – La respuesta de trabajadores inmigrantes

The national political landscape has changed. The election results have altered the balance of political power and could open new opportunities for negotiations. But it would be a serious mistake to interpret this new political environment as a guarantee of immigration reform. The great achievements in civil, labor, and social rights in the United States have not resulted exclusively from the goodwill of those occupying the White House. They have been the product of long struggles involving organization, mobilization, and collective action.

Those of us who have devoted more than forty years to defending immigrant workers’ rights must maintain our political independence, determination, and constant vigilance. We cannot place our hopes in Trump’s declarations or make our strategy dependent on his shifting political rhetoric. Our task is to strengthen immigrant workers’ organizations and expand our alliances with labor unions, community organizations, religious institutions, and civil rights advocates.

We must build the broadest possible unity among U.S. citizen workers, lawful permanent residents, and undocumented workers. They all share fundamental interests: decent wages, fair working conditions, family stability, and respect for their human rights. Dividing American citizen workers from immigrant workers benefits only those who seek to weaken their collective ability to defend those rights.

Not even a little bit! – ¡Ni un Poquito!

This does not mean rejecting in advance every possibility of negotiating with Donald Trump. If he presents a serious, concrete, and verifiable proposal that opens a path toward permanent legalization for millions of undocumented workers, it should be examined responsibly. But we must not confuse a willingness to engage in dialogue with an obligation to believe. ‘Como decía mi abuelita, ver para creer’.

After a decade of broken promises, contradictions, and restrictive immigration policies, the burden rests on the president to demonstrate that this time his words mean something different. The burden of proof rests with him, not with the millions of immigrants who have waited decades for a just solution.

Undocumented workers do not need another presidential promise. They need rights, stability, and the opportunity to live without the constant fear that their families will be torn apart – again.

After more than forty years of struggle, we cannot settle for anything less.

Let us listen to what Trump says now. Let us examine what he proposes. But above all, let us judge what he does. Because when it comes to Donald Trump’s promises on immigration reform, we cannot afford to trust him, not even a little, ‘ni un poquito.’
