text:
Chris Van Hollen has suggested John Fetterman may be "looking for an exit ramp" from the Democratic Party after the Pennsylvania senator criticized his bid for Senate leadership.

On Fox News Sunday, the Maryland Democrat responded after Fetterman said it would be "troubling" if his caucus elected Van Hollen as its leader because of what he described as the senator's hostility toward Israel.

Van Hollen defended his positions on Israel and Kilmar Abrego Garcia, arguing that neither foreign governments nor the Donald Trump administration should receive a "blank check" when constitutional or legal principles are at stake.

Read More on Politics

Kilmar Abrego Garcia is a Salvadoran national who was deported from the United States to El Salvador despite a court order that barred his removal there. His case became a major legal battle over President Trump's immigration policies, eventually reaching the Supreme Court, which backed a lower court order requiring the government to facilitate his return to the United States.

Newsweek contacted Van Hollen and Fetterman's representatives via email for comment on Sunday.

Why It Matters

Fetterman has increasingly broken with fellow Democrats on Israel and other issues, but has previously rejected suggestions that he plans to become a Republican.

Van Hollen's response turns their policy disagreement into a broader political question by openly suggesting his Pennsylvania colleague could be considering a way out of the party.

What To Know

Van Hollen Responds To Fetterman

Appearing on Fox News Sunday on November 15, Van Hollen began by highlighting an area where he said the two senators could agree.

"First of all, I hope Senator Fetterman will stay true to his economic populist message, and that's something that I would support," Van Hollen said.

He then turned to Fetterman's political future.

"It's widely known that Senator Fetterman is worried about a Democratic primary in his state of Pennsylvania. And so maybe looking for an exit ramp," Van Hollen added.

His comments responded to an interview a day earlier, in which Fetterman was asked by Kayleigh McEnany whether electing Van Hollen as Senate majority leader could become a red line that prompted him to leave the party.

"Yeah, absolutely, it would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen, that has really made his name being very...hostile to Israel," Fetterman said.

Israel at the Center of the Dispute

Van Hollen rejected Fetterman's characterization of his approach to Israel, framing his position instead around conditions on U.S. taxpayer support.

"My position is that American taxpayers should not be providing a blank check to the government of Israel or any government, regardless of their conduct," he said.

Van Hollen also pointed specifically to violence involving Israeli settlers in the West Bank, saying U.S. money should not support such conduct.

His record has put him among the Senate's more prominent Democratic critics of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government. In November 2024, he backed resolutions seeking to block some offensive weapons sales while continuing to support Israel's right to defend itself and U.S. transfers of defensive systems, including Iron Dome.

Abrego Garcia Becomes Another Flashpoint

Van Hollen also addressed Fetterman's criticism of his advocacy for the constitutional rights of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose removal to El Salvador became a prominent dispute over the Trump administration's immigration policies.

He argued that the case had implications beyond one individual.

"The American people? They're actually with me because they understand it's not just about one man. It's about the constitutional rights of everybody," Van Hollen said. "If you take his away, you've threatened them for everybody."

Democratic Leadership Fight Looms

The confrontation comes as Van Hollen challenges Chuck Schumer for the party's top Senate leadership role following Democrats' midterm victories.

Van Hollen announced his challenge Thursday, arguing voters had demanded change in Washington.

"In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption," he wrote on X. "To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person–it's about answering that call."

Van Hollen has publicly described himself as the underdog, saying his campaign is focused on closing what he calls a "trust deficit" between Americans and political leaders. Schumer, meanwhile, has reportedly expressed confidence that he has enough backing to retain the position.

Fetterman's Future Draws Scrutiny

Despite his clashes with Democrats, Fetterman has previously pushed back on the idea that he intends to switch parties.

In a May Washington Post opinion piece, he called himself a "terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats."

Speculation has nevertheless reached prediction markets. Kalshi traders gave Fetterman a 23 percent implied chance of becoming the Republican Senate nominee in Pennsylvania in 2028 as of 1 p.m. ET on November 14, compared with 32 percent for Representative Brian Fitzpatrick. A separate market put his implied chance of winning the Democratic nomination at 3 percent.

Prediction market odds reflect the prices traders are willing to pay on a particular outcome and should be viewed as a measure of speculative market sentiment, rather than as polling or evidence that a candidate has filed to run.

For now, Van Hollen's suggestion that his colleague could be seeking an "exit ramp" also remains speculation rather than evidence that Fetterman has decided to leave the Democratic Party.

text:
The Trump administration has asked the US Supreme Court to further restrict federal judges’ authority to block government policies nationwide, escalating a legal battle over presidential power and judicial oversight.

Reuters reported on November 14, 2026, that the Justice Department had appealed to the Supreme Court to limit judges’ longstanding power to invalidate federal agency regulations across the country. The move could give President Donald Trump greater freedom to implement his policy agenda by making it harder for courts to suspend government rules beyond the individuals or organisations that challenge them.

The appeal targets a legal mechanism under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), a 1946 law governing federal agencies and their regulations. Courts have traditionally interpreted the legislation as allowing judges to strike down agency rules they find unlawful, with decisions sometimes applying nationwide rather than being limited to the parties involved in a lawsuit.

The administration argues that judges should not have the authority to invalidate federal regulations universally and that any relief should generally be restricted to the specific plaintiffs who bring legal challenges.

The latest effort follows a significant Supreme Court ruling in June 2025 that curtailed the use of nationwide injunctions. Those orders had allowed federal judges to prevent the government from enforcing policies against people beyond those directly involved in lawsuits.

The ruling was a major victory for Trump, whose administration has faced hundreds of legal challenges over immigration restrictions, mass deportations, diversity programmes and policies affecting transgender rights since returning to office in January 2025.

However, the 2025 decision did not resolve the separate question of whether courts could invalidate federal agency regulations nationwide under the APA. The administration is now seeking to extend those restrictions to this additional judicial power.

The distinction is important because the Supreme Court’s June 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA restricted nationwide injunctions but explicitly left open the question of nationwide invalidation of federal agency rules under the APA. A Congressional Research Service analysis published in July 2026 also highlighted that the ruling had left this separate form of judicial relief unresolved.

Legal analysts say the administration’s latest appeal could have consequences far beyond the dispute over medical billing. Bloomberg Law reported in October that a decision favouring the government could affect a broad range of regulatory challenges, including cases involving the Affordable Care Act, Medicare and Medicaid.

A ruling in Trump’s favour could allow federal agencies to continue enforcing regulations against the wider public even after courts have found them unlawful, while legal challenges proceed. Critics argue that restricting nationwide remedies could weaken an important judicial safeguard against executive overreach and make it harder to ensure federal rules are applied consistently across the country.

text:
About 200 people have been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Hawaiʻi so far this year, according to The Legal Clinic.

In reaction to the ramped up enforcement under the Trump administration, the Hawai’i State Legislature passed six major immigration bills earlier this year that strengthen protections for Hawai‘i’s immigrant community.

In preparation for the rollout of the laws in 2027, the Campaign for Immigrant Justice that advocated for the new laws has embarked on a “Due Process Roadshow,” which seeks to educate local organizations and law enforcement about them.

On Thursday, the roadshow arrived on the Big Island, hosted by Hawaiʻi County Council member Jenn Kagiwada.

“It’s very important to have all the information on these new laws for our local officials and the community who may not be aware just yet,” Kagiwada said. “I hope this helps open a dialogue between the community and government entities when it comes to these changes.”

The roadshow included representatives from the Hawaiʻi Coalition for Immigrant Rights, the ACLU of Hawaiʻi and The Legal Clinic, an organization that offers high-quality immigration legal services, education, and advocacy for low-income immigrants and migrants in Hawaiʻi.

Liza Ryan Gill, executive director for the Hawaiʻi Coalition for Immigrant Rights, said it is important that individuals, agencies and departments “really understand how these new laws need to be implemented on the ground. That is why we are here.”

According to the coalition, the six bills that were signed this year came from about 42 bills relating to immigration and due process that were introduced this year in the last legislative session.

The six immigration bills that were passed this year:

Act 141: Prohibits any law enforcement agency or official from entering a federal agreement that permits state or county agencies to engage in immigration enforcement. Prohibits certain immigration-related actions except under limited circumstances.

Act 142: Establishes uniform statewide requirements for U and T visa certifications for noncitizen victims of crime, consistent with federal law. Every state and county certifying entity must adopt an aligned, timely, transparent policy and process.

Act 143: Limits the maximum term of imprisonment for misdemeanors that are not crimes of violence to 364 days. Allows individuals previously sentenced to one year for non-violent offenses to apply for sentence reconsideration.

Act 161: Requires state and county law enforcement to notify any individual in custody of their rights before any interview with federal immigration authorities about civil immigration violations can begin. Makes records of federal immigration access to detained individuals public records.

Act 162: Requires all state and county agencies operating protected community locations — schools, hospitals, courthouses, libraries, shelters — to identify nonpublic areas and post written policies by January 1, 2027. Establishes warrant verification procedures, prohibits collection of certain immigration-status data, and requires annual training.

Act 179: Establishes a Language Access Education and Workforce Development Program at the University of Hawaiʻi and positions and funds at UH Mānoa, Leeward Community College, and Kapiʻolani Community College. Builds a pipeline of certified interpreters for state services in Hawaiʻi’s most-spoken languages.

Kagiwada said the state laws establish consequences and consistent policy that should be followed by state and county agencies.

For example, Act 141 — which prohibits any law enforcement agency or official from entering a federal agreement that permits state or county agencies to engage in immigration enforcement —passed because Hawaiʻi had no statewide rule. Each agency was left to decide how to responded to ICE, including whether to sign an agreement that would deputize officers for immigration functions. The bill gives Hawaiʻi’s agencies one consistent policy of noncooperation.

While the Hawaiʻi Police Department does not have any outstanding formal agreements with ICE, there have been reports of informal cooperation with civil immigration enforcement.

Act 142 involves the protection of crime survivors and encourages cooperation with law enforcement. It establishes a set certification practice for U visas, which were created for victims of certain serious crimes who help law enforcement, and T visas, which were created for survivors of human trafficking.

“Survivors of crimes are more willing to come forward when they trust the legal system and know they can cooperate without fear of immigration consequences,” Gill said.

Act 143 shortens Hawaiʻi’s maximum misdemeanor sentence from one-year to 364 days due to the life-altering immigration consequences that are triggered once a lawful permanent resident, an undocumented resident or even residents under the Compact of Free Association (from Micronesia, Marshall Islands and Palau) reaches a 365 day sentence.

Reducing the maximum by a single day removes that trigger without changing the seriousness of the offense.

The Hawaiʻi County Office of the Prosecuting Attorney should now apply the 364-day maximum in charging, plea and sentencing, and courts should prepare for sentence-modification applications from people sentenced before the Act and adjust any publicly available information about sentencing modification.

Act 161 requires that people in state or county custody must be told their rights, in a language they understand, before any federal civil immigration interview, including the right to have their attorney present and to decline the interview. ICE is granted access only with the person’s written consent.

Violations can be brought to the Attorney General or county prosecutors; people whose due process rights are violated may sue.

“If ICE breaks any of these laws, then the person involved has a much better case to fight against detainment or deportation,” said Bettina Mok, executive director for The Legal Clinic. “This bill ensures that everyone has the right to due process despite any language barriers.”

This bill requires the state and counties to prepare rights-notice forms with translations in the languages commonly encountered in each facility. It also requires the establishment of a protocol for how ICE interview requests are received, logged and routed.

According to the Hawaiʻi Coalition for Immigrant Rights, Act 162 requires the most action from county agencies and law enforcement. The bill requires protected community locations to identify nonpublic areas, set procedures for warrant verification, prohibits collecting immigration data, requires annual staff training and requires the posting of multilingual notices.

“Before the second Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security did not conduct operations at sensitive locations, like hospitals, schools, weddings, libraries, shelters and churches,” said Mandy Fernandes, policy director for ACLU Hawaiʻi. “They threw that out and we had a few incidences of ICE going into K to 12 spaces and hospitals, so this bill is a response to that.”

The Attorney General must publish model policies for state and county agencies to adopt, and for private operators like schools and churches to adopt voluntarily.

“We cannot stop ICE from going into a school, but we can have somebody that has been appointed the person to review whatever the document is that they’re coming with and ascertain whether or not it is a judicial warrant,” Fernandes said. “We’re also asking that state and county facilities designate what is a private space and what is a public space. As an example, the front desk of a health center is public, the exam rooms are private.”

According to the coalition, this type of legislation has been passed in at least 10 states, so they are gathering the best kind of uses for it and the Hawaiʻi Attorney General will be putting out guidelines before January 1.

“I’ll be trying to talk to different departments and the mayoral administration about the counties role in offering training and what we can do to help with these sensitive locations,” Kagiwada said.

Then, Act 179 passed because agencies often cannot find enough qualified interpreters and translators, and interviews of victims and witnesses, domestic violence calls, traffic stops, and rights advisements all depend on accurate communication.

The law requires language access education and workforce development program at the University of Hawaiʻi with priority for high school graduates who earn the Department of Education’s Seal of Biliteracy and for community members with demonstrated biliteracy.

The program will train in ethics, standards, best practices, specialized instruction and opportunities in public service settings. Funding will be divided among UH Mānoa, Leeward Community College and Kapiʻolani Community College.

One of the 42 bills that did not pass the legislative session was the creation of infrastrucutre and funding to support the right to a public defender in immigration court.

At the federal level, the Immigration and Nationality Act does not give individuals in removal proceedings the right to be represented by an attorney for free, but only at their own expense.

As a result, most people who cannot afford an attorney – including an estimated 70 percent of those in immigration detention – are left to fend for themselves in navigating the complexities of immigration law while facing highly-trained government attorneys.

“At the state and county level, there are ways to support access to justice and make sure those who are facing deportation or seeking asylum have pathways to legal status,” Fernandes said. “However, there are maybe a dozen immigration attorneys statewide and we know we need to build that network. The Legal Clinic is one of the few pro bono services available for low-income immigrants.”

Hawaiʻi County is working to combat the lack of immigration lawyers by making immigration specialists available in East Hawaiʻi and West Hawaiʻi.

“We did have an East Hawaiʻi public defender here earlier and he was saying that makes a huge difference from him personally since he is not an immigration specialist,” Kagiwada said. “He needs the resources in his office so when these things come up with this clients, he can make sure he’s doing the right thing for them.”

The Immigration Information Office provides assistance on immigration related issues and concerns to the constituents of Hawaiʻi County, disseminates immigration forms, acts as a resource office, and serves as a liaison to the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services.

There is currently an Immigration Information Office in Hilo.

According to Kagiwada, the County of Hawaiʻi is currently searching for a part-time immigration specialist for West Hawaiʻi, but believes there is a need to have at least one full-time employee available.

In addition to the public presentations, coalition organizers are planning to meet separately with leaders of the agencies charged with implementing these new laws, including county police, prosecutors, corporation counsel and administrators.

text:
President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline travel this weekend, using the incident to push Congress on money to fully upgrade America's air traffic control system.

The Republican president has been quiet on the ground stop since it began Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.

Trump said in a new post on his social media platform that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in "drips and drabs." The Republican-controlled Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Federal Aviation Administration as part of the party's sweeping tax cut package last year, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly characterized that funding as an down payment on a broader overhaul of the aging system.

"If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," Trump wrote on social media Sunday. "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!"

MORE | Ground Stop:

Passengers face lingering delays as Salt Lake Airport recovers from nationwide ground stop

Intermountain suspends fixed-wing medical requests during FAA ground stop

Nationwide ground stop ends after FAA lifts order barring flights from taking off

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing Joe Biden's administration of making an "old and broken system worse than when they began."

Biden signed a massive infrastructure bill into law in the first year of his presidency, which set aside $25 billion for the FAA to improve airports and its traffic control towers, to redevelop airport terminals, to "upgrade the foundation" of the air traffic control system, according to the FAA.

Duffy was the administration's public face on the ground stop across the Sunday news shows, pressing Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air traffic control infrastructure.

In a post on the social media platform X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. had secured two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting "deep diagnostics" on the equipment. He has said the problem began when L3Harris was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload.

After the wire was replaced at the site in El Dorado, Ark., and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, cascading into the ground stop. "We didn't think that should or would happen, he told ABC's "This Week."

As for the traveling public, he told CBS' "Face the Nation" that "we have some delays in the airspace right now," but looking to the end of the day and into Monday, "we should be running at full capacity."

In a ground stop, airplanes and crews are taken out of position, he said, "so it takes a little bit of time for the airliners to get back at full capacity and operation but we're well on our way."

title: 'Shameless venality': how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump's self-enrichment schemes
description:
Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.
The major lawsuits against Trump’s financial ploys have been the handiwork of several nonpartisan groups including Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center.
In response, judges in Florida and New York used strong language to condemn and help nullify some of Trump’s financial stratagems.
One of the ads echoed Trump’s dubious claim that if Republicans maintained control of Congress, all Americans would receive $5,000.
We can’t count on his own conscience, ethics or advisers to check his worst instincts, but the courts have seen through his various schemes, from his slush fund to his use of taxpayer funds for political ads.”
text:
Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.

Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat.

The major lawsuits against Trump’s financial ploys have been the handiwork of several nonpartisan groups including Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center.

In response, judges in Florida and New York used strong language to condemn and help nullify some of Trump’s financial stratagems. Florida judge Kathleen Williams castigated a Trump scheme backed by the justice department to settle a $10bn lawsuit he filed against the Internal Revenue Service over an old leak of his tax information to the New York Times.

Williams ruled that the Trump backed deal to set up a $1.8bn slush fund to pay alleged victims of political persecutions under Joe Biden and giving him immunity from IRS audits before May 2026 was “premised on deception” and a “fraud against the court”.

In a separate legal blow to Trump in the closing weeks of the campaign, the president was rebuked by a federal judge in New York, for channeling $20m of public funds to run ads touting his administration’s achievements. The ads were widely attacked as campaign ads and propaganda.

Former judges and ex-DoJ lawyers say that he Trump moves to boost his bottom line and political drives with backing from DoJ lawyers exemplify various kinds of Trump “corruption”.

Stacey Young, a former DoJ lawyer who set up Justice Connection last year as a network to defend the justice department workforce and the rule of law, told the Guardian: “The justice department’s leadership believes it has one chief client: President Trump. They have allowed him to use the department to protect his financial interests, punish his enemies, and reward his friends.

“Thanks to the efforts of some of the country’s best litigators, the people of the United States are pushing back and standing up for the ideal that we remain a government of laws, not of men.”

Further, retired federal appeals court judge J Michael Luttig said: “The courts have recently begun to strike down Trump’s countless schemes of blatant and shameless venality and corruption in the forms of self-enrichment, bribery, and extortion. That is the through-line of these three cases and the numerous other cases to come.”

For Luttig, the court rebuffs are part of a broader trend of federal courts also rejecting as unconstitutional major presidential initiatives including tariffs and birthright citizenship.

Luttig’s analysis was underscored by a July lawsuit filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and a coalition of 35 ex-judges, including Luttig, to kill a key piece of Trump’s proposed settlement of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS by establishing a $1.8bn fund to pay alleged victims of political persecution that could have helped some January 6 Capitol rioters.

The DoJ dropped the slush-fund idea after Williams ruling and some political blowback by Congress. But despite Williams’s legal objections and sharp criticism from Democratic senators, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, a provision is still in effect providing immunity to Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from investigations and prosecutions of past tax matters by the IRS as compensation over a leak of his tax returns.

In her ruling, Williams charged that the plaintiffs initiated the lawsuit “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”.

Williams’s scathing opinion in mid-July noted that Trump was on both sides of the issue and that the court itself was perhaps “the victim of fraud”. Williams concluded that the plaintiffs had acted in bad faith by “collusively filing a lawsuit with claims subject to multiple dispositive defenses solely to provide cover for a collusive settlement”.

Citing language from an earlier ruling, Williams said “this case is part of Mr Trump’s pattern of misusing the courts to serve political purposes”. In summary, Williams wrote, acidly, that the plaintiffs “pursued this lawsuit in bad faith for the improper purpose of dishonestly advancing a political narrative”.

Trump’s lawyers in late July said they would appeal the Williams order. In late September, a federal appeals court for the 11th circuit rejected a request from Trump and his lawyers to immediately lift sanctions that Williams imposed in response to the settlement Trump and the DoJ backed over the leak of his tax returns.

In its ruling, the appeals court denied a request by two Trump lawyers, Alejandro Brito and Daniel Epstein, to pause sanctions against them over their handling of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS. The court ruled the lawyers had not demonstrated they would succeed in challenging finding that they acted in bad faith.

In another legal blow for Trump, two restraining orders were issued in October by district judge Jennifer Rochon in New York to stop his use of public funds for financing campaign style ads after Campaign Legal Center Action representing Common Cause, along with Public Integrity Project Action and Democracy Forward sued.

In her second emergency order on 30 October, Judge Rochon ruled that three ads could no longer run using government funds on Instagram and two other sites since they were “purely partisan” .

One of the ads echoed Trump’s dubious claim that if Republicans maintained control of Congress, all Americans would receive $5,000. The three ads Rochon ordered removed were headlined “$5,000 to Americans” the “Cost of Socialism” and “Every Democrat Voted against No Tax on Tips”.

Shortly before Rochon’s first ruling, Trump in a Truth Social post on 5 October defended using government funds for the ads and blithely stated that tapping public funds was “rather standard”.

But with growing criticism, including from some Republicans, Trump announced he would pay for them himself from his political fundraising operation. The justice department also tried to forestall the first restraining order by asserting that “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow”.

Renata O’Donnell, a senior legal counsel with Campaign Legal Center who worked on the case, told the Guardian: “The Department of Homeland Security used $20m in taxpayer dollars to pay a private ad agency for airtime for government-created propaganda. This is blatantly illegal.”

O’Donnell added: “In direct violation of the law, White House staff, whose salaries are paid with taxpayer dollars, were creating propaganda, including ads that promised people $5,000 to vote Republican.”

In another pending legal battle that courts have yet to rule on, Democracy Defenders Fund filed a lawsuit with the San Francisco city attorney, the Washington Litigation Group and Platkin LLP to block a Trump financial gambit to offer special early access to his Truth Social posts to users who pay a fee as high as $100,000 per month to the parent company of Truth Social.

The lawsuit was filed in mid-September against Trump Media and Technology Group, which operates and owns Truth Social.

San Francisco city attorney David Chiu asked the San Francisco superior court to bar Trump Media from offering its new service, dubbed “Trump API”, or a similar one, plus provide monetary damages for violating the public trust and the state’s unfair competition law.

“Trump Media created a marketplace that enables insider trading, which Trump directly profits from,” Chiu said in a statement. “This scheme turns the public trust into private profit. It is corruption, plain and simple.”

A Trump Media spokesperson ridiculed the lawsuit when it was filed, charging that “the people of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the leftwing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information”.

David Ogden, a senior counsel with DDF who has worked on the case, noted that “Congress made clear that the president, like any public servant, shouldn’t be permitted to profiteer off of special access to government information. It’s a violation of the public trust and it’s important that it be stopped.”

In the eyes of Barbara McQuade, former US attorney for eastern Michigan, who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, the different court rulings against Trump’s financial ploys reveal his penchant for “personal enrichment” and political ploys during his presidency.

“It seems that Trump has no shame about using his office for personal enrichment. We can’t count on his own conscience, ethics or advisers to check his worst instincts, but the courts have seen through his various schemes, from his slush fund to his use of taxpayer funds for political ads.”

text:
Senate Bill 873 prohibits federal law enforcement agents from making civil arrests within 1,000 feet of a courthouse without a judicial warrant.

Representatives from the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office and County Counsel's office said they do not believe the bill precludes civil arrests inside the jail’s lobby.

Other local leaders, however, are hopeful that the law will apply to the main jail.

The impact of a new state law prohibiting federal law enforcement agents from making civil arrests within 1,000 feet of courthouses without judicial warrants is largely unclear in Ventura County.

California Senate Bill 873, which takes effect Jan. 1, is an effort to protect undocumented immigrants’ access to the judicial system.

However, in places like Ventura County, where the main jail is a frequent location for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers' arrest of undocumented immigrants, the law does not include language regarding civil arrests at jails within the 1,000-foot zone of the courts.

The California Attorney General's Office as well as the office of one of bill's co-authors did not provide The Star with information on how the bill might impact jails.

Representatives from the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office and County of Ventura’s County Counsel told The Star they do not believe the bill precludes civil arrests inside the jail’s release lobby.

Other local leaders, however, are hopeful that the law will apply to the main jail and when it takes effect Jan. 1 it will lead to an increased sense of safety among undocumented immigrants.

“It is important to ensure we are following the laws that are in place because the laws are informed by the community,” Ventura County Supervisor Vianey Lopez said. “I see this bill as another way to ensure that our communities are welcoming of everyone in the community, no matter who they are or where they came from.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions.

About the bill

Existing California law prohibits a person from being subject to civil arrest inside a courthouse without a federal judicial warrant, and Senate Bill 873 extends that protection to 1,000 feet outside of the courthouse.

Kate Chatfield, executive director of the California Public Defenders Association — a cosponsor of the bill — said her staff has witnessed an increase in ICE agents apprehending undocumented immigrants as they enter and exit court, even dragging them out of their cars in the parking lots.

That deters many of her clients from attending court, harming not only the undocumented immigrant community but also democracy, she said.

“If people are afraid to go to court, they essentially have no access to their own judicial system,” she said. “A functioning democracy requires a functioning judicial system."

The law focuses on court proceedings and does not mention jails, though Chatfield said if a county’s jail is within 1,000 feet from its courthouse, civil arrests inside or immediately outside of the jail would also violate the law, as there are no exceptions.

Allison Westcott, communications director for State Sen. Eloise Gómez Reyes, who co-authored the bill, said her office deferred the interpretation of the bill as it relates to jails to the attorney general's office as it would be responsible for enforcement.

A spokesperson for the AG's office, however, said that the agency was unable to provide any legal analysis.

Civil arrests that violate the bill would constitute false imprisonment, and individuals who either violate or assist in the violation of the bill would be liable for civil damages of $10,000.

The bill would require court security to request that the law enforcement agents who enter the courthouse identify themselves and the enforcement action they intend to take and request a copy of their required judicial warrant. If court personnel are aware the person named in the warrant has an attorney, they must request that the agents allow the attorney to review the warrant.

The bill does not, however, require the federal agents to present their warrant to anyone unless security personnel requests it. Chatfield said she is aware that many courthouses do not have security personnel outside the building. That, she said, is one of the limitations of enforcing the law.

“It would be an area of improvement,” she said of the enforcement aspect.

Chatfield said they have to be cognizant of federal laws that override contradicting state laws, often referred to is federal preemption.

She said she feels the Legislature and governor are doing what they can within the limitations that exist to resist ICE and protect residents.

“I hope it will be effective,” Chatfield said.

Local interpretation

Though California law largely prohibits local and state law enforcement agencies from assisting federal immigration enforcement agencies, it gives them the option to notify ICE when certain individuals — such as those convicted of or held to answer for robbery, residential burglary or rape — are released from jail.

The sheriff’s office voluntarily cooperates with ICE, and during the Oct. 20 TRUTH Act forum, Fryhoff said that of the office’s roughly 169 notifications to ICE in 2025, federal agents picked up 114 individuals from the jail — more than double the number picked up in either of the previous two years.

When Lopez asked Fryhoff how SB 873 would be enforced locally, he confirmed the jail was roughly 100 or 200 yards from the court but suggested the law could be overturned in federal court.

“If you look at all the other laws that the state has created to try and limit federal authority, they've all been overturned by the courts; they have no standing to tell the federal government what to do…” Fryhoff told Lopez. “Your choice will be to break the law or break the law.”

Wescott, however, said Gómez Reyes worked closely with Attorney General Rob Bonta's Office on the bill's language and has full confidence in the office's ability to enforce the law, citing his recent lawsuit challenging ICE's arrests at courthouses.

In separate emails, Capt. Robert Yoos, sheriff’s office spokesperson, and Tiffany North, county counsel, said their agencies do not believe the SB 873 prohibits ICE arrests in the main jail’s release lobby.

“The arrests they are making are unrelated to a scheduled court appearance and thus do not prevent anyone from attending court to address a legal matter,” Yoos wrote.

However, if an incident in the location appeared to violate the law, the sheriff’s office would document it and submit it to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office or the California Department of Justice for review, he said.

In an interview, Lopez said she understands that many Ventura County residents’ sense of safety has been impacted by the sheriff’s office’s voluntary cooperation with ICE.

“I am hopeful that we can work to create safer spaces and perhaps gain some trust from the community,” she said.

Volunteer documentation

Willie Lubka, the executive director of immigration advocacy nonprofit Buen Vecino and a representative of ICE Out of Ventura County, said he supports Senate Bill 873 because he knows that a significant number of undocumented immigrants in Ventura County are not showing up to the Ventura County Superior Court because of the frequency of ICE’s presence in the government center and wants to prevent that.

He said he was upset that Fryhoff did not commit to enforcing Senate Bill 873 during the forum.

“We expect him to maintain his posture of being an enforcer of the law, and he should observe and enforce this law just like he would any other,” he said.

Buen Vecino’s volunteers work closely with other nonprofits that serve the region’s immigrant community, such as VC Defensa and 805 UndocuFund, to not only protest ICE arrests inside the jail lobby but also observe and document them.

He said it is likely that the volunteers will measure the 1,000 feet circumference around the court building and document any civil arrests that occur within that circumference to send to the DA's Office or the attorney general in order to hold accountable both federal and local officers who are involved or present.

Lubka said it is unfortunate that the enforcement aspect of the law is not stronger and that even if the sheriff’s office and court personnel do enforce the law, the ICE agents can simply wait just beyond the 1,000 feet mark to make their arrests.

“It’s not, unfortunately, all that uncommon when there’s a law that is a law but there’s no specific … enforcement mechanisms, which make a law much weaker,” he said. “I would rather have that than what they’re doing now.”

But the Trump administration has trampled on that essential feature of our constitutional republic in its anti-immigrant crusade. Again and again, the administration has defied the courts, either by ignoring judicial rulings outright or by doing end runs around them.

Once upon a time we would have called this a constitutional crisis. Somehow, it has become business as usual in President Donald J. Trump’s Washington.

The latest instances, as documented by The New York Times: The administration has been deporting immigrants back to their home countries even in cases where it’s illegal to do so because American courts had determined they would face torture, sexual abuse or persecution. Fleeing that fate is what brought them to the U.S. in search of asylum.

The government accomplished this workaround by handing off the individuals to a different foreign government on the understanding they would then send them back home. Those third parties, many with poor human rights records, aren’t subject to U.S. court orders.

The Times identified more than 110 such people who had court-ordered protections but who ended up back in their home countries nonetheless.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A nongovernmental organization, Human Rights First, found at least 310 people who’d been under court-ordered protection but were deported nonetheless to third countries. At least 114 of them were then transferred to their countries of origin.

According to Human Rights First, they included people who had fled anti-LGBTQ violence and other harms, female genital mutilation, forced marriage, religious persecution and hereditary slavery.

In some cases, the group found, the Trump administration sent people directly to their home countries in open violation of the court order, without even bothering with the ruse of an intermediary nation.

One such case made national news earlier this year: The administration flew Kilmar Abrego Garcia to be imprisoned in a notorious prison in El Salvador even after a judge expressly told it not to. The administration said the judge’s order wasn’t in writing, so there.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

On the practice of sending people to third countries, the administration’s says it doesn’t track what happens to people after they’re deported. That implausible denial makes the government all the more responsible for willful negligence.

Not only is the administration violating the court protections for these individuals, but it’s defying a district court ruling that found its practice of deporting people to third countries illegal. The Supreme Court’s conservative majority, however, granted the administration’s request for a stay of the lower court’s order on Sept. 29, allowing it to continue the practice until the high court rules on its legality.

Though the ruling will likely result in irreparable harm to some deportees — harm that no possible future decision in their favor will be able to fix — it’s sadly in keeping with the court’s leniency toward the administration’s abuses of human rights and defiance of lower courts.

And it’s important to note that this deportation practice isn’t occurring in isolation. It’s a piece of a broader pattern of defiance of the courts that has led a number of judges around the country to question whether government lawyers can still be implicitly trusted to be acting in good faith, following legal norms and presenting facts.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It’s unlikely that the administration will change its ways without strong pressure from Congress. Come January, Republicans who have either cheered on Mr. Trump’s cruelty or looked the other way will be out of power, and Democrats will hold majorities in both the House and Senate. It’s essential that the next Congress conduct meaningful oversight of this practice and the entire immigration system with an eye toward reforming it — from the poor vetting of Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits, to ICE’s abuses of civil and human rights, to the question of whether administrative immigration courts, now under the executive branch, should be part of the independent judicial branch.

The rule of law is based on a simple but profound proposition: that everyone, even the government and the powerful people within it, is equal under the law. That means equally protected and equally accountable. A Congress under Mr. Trump’s thumb has let his administration’s abuses of the rule of law slide for far too long. When the new Congress is sworn it, it will be time to rebalance the scales of justice.

The people who died in the Flatbush building collapse came from opposite ends of the world. But their loved ones said they shared the same hope: to make a new life in New York City.

“We have no words,” Juan Carlos Zabala said of his lost family. “They were following the American dream.”

His cousin, Juan Daniel Sabala, 31, had a 9-year-old daughter, Nicole. Both died in the wreckage. Another cousin of the same family, 10-year-old Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, was also found dead.

The collapse killed five other New Yorkers and injured 18 more in what is among the worst residential building collapses in recent city history. Zabala — speaking to Gothamist from Spain — said Friday that his cousin’s wife was still hospitalized and receiving intensive care with the couple’s 3-year-old daughter. Many others were also waiting for updates from their surviving family and friends.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin read the names of the dead, beginning with Sabala and his daughter, during a news conference Friday at a shelter for the displaced.

“They were cousins, they were roommates, they were sons, they were daughters, they were children,” Menin said. “They were Juan Sabala and Gabriel Siguencia, and two cousins who lived together, Mamadou Ndiaye and Mamadou Barry. They were Nicole Sabala and Kevin Reyes, another set of young cousins. They were Edgar Sapon, a construction worker who leaves a wife and 6-year-old son. They were José Caguana, who would pick up his 4-year-old son from preschool, and his wife is expecting a second child soon.”

Zabala said the family had arrived in the country three or four years ago, and Sabala had been working for a cleaning company. But the last time they spoke, Zabala said, his cousin sounded anxious.

“Everything with ICE was really bothering them,” he said. “So they stayed shut inside, from work to home and home to work because they were afraid of being deported.”

The family was home on Wednesday because it was Veterans Day, Zabala said. He had been planning to come visit in December — but now was left processing what had become of his relatives.

“I have a lot of nostalgia and a lot of sadness … because I am also in another country that’s not mine,” he said. “We came with a dream, hoping for a better life. And at the end, we don’t know what will happen to us.”

Ndiaye and Barry shared their apartment with a married couple, Mamadou Mouctar Balde and his wife, Fatoumata Binta Bah. She is six months pregnant and was pulled from the rubble by emergency workers. A widely shared picture of the rescue by AP Photographer Ryan Murphy shows her lying on a stretcher, flanked by firefighters, her skin caked with white dust.

She remains hospitalized with serious injuries, according to Councilmember Farah Louis, but she and her baby survived.

Balde, speaking in French, said he’d left the apartment to buy groceries shortly before the building collapsed. When he came back, emergency services and the Red Cross were already there. He thought there’d been a traffic accident until a woman told him the building had come down.

“When she told me there had been a collapse, I didn’t know where I was anymore, because I know our building borders that site,” Balde said. He said he told the woman, “My wife is inside, my friends are inside.”

Two of the dead, Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia Yupa and José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, were construction workers from Ecuador. Caguana Cosquillo’s wife is set to give birth this weekend, said Winston Sanchez, who spoke on behalf of the men’s families.

“It is a sad day because it not only collapsed the building, it collapsed the lives of many relatives, brothers, fathers,” Sanchez said.

Investigations into what led to the collapse are underway. Attorney General Letitia James said she was standing ready to help however she can.

“The families in this community deserve answers about what led to this collapse,” James said.

Louis, who at one point struggled to hold back tears, went further:

“Buildings do not simply collapse without systemic failure,” she said, adding that records show “a building with nearly 100 open violations sitting next to an excavation site cited for violating a stop work order.”

The speakers noted that the mayor’s office has set up an emergency relief fund for those affected, and the Flatbush YMCA is collecting gift cards and checks. Other organizations have stepped up to collect donations as well.

text:
The median immigration bond in Denver reached $20,000 in September, more than 13 times the $1,500 median in Bloomington, Minnesota, according to newly released court data showing a sharp geographic divide in the cost of securing release from detention.

The analysis by the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, published Oct. 26, put the national median at $7,500. Denver's figure also held at $20,000 across fiscal 2026, while Bloomington's full-year median was $3,000.

Immigration judges granted bond to 2,646 people in September, the largest monthly total in two years. They held just under 10,000 bond hearings that month. Mexican nationals accounted for the largest number of hearings in both cities and about a quarter of bond grants nationwide during the fiscal year, followed nationally by Guatemalans and Venezuelans.

The $18,500 difference between the two September medians raises questions about how custody decisions translate into financial hurdles for immigrants and their families. The report does not establish how much of the gap reflects individual circumstances, differences in the cases reaching each court, or local decision-making.

Bond proceedings determine whether eligible immigrants can leave custody while their immigration cases continue. The Justice Department's immigration court practice manual explains that the Department of Homeland Security initially sets bond, and an immigration judge may reconsider it at the detained person's request.

Judges consider eligibility, potential danger to people or property, the likelihood of appearing for future proceedings and national security concerns. Some categories of detainees fall outside judges' bond jurisdiction.

Requests generally go to the court responsible for the place of detention. There is no filing fee to request a bond hearing. That hearing is separate from the proceeding that determines whether someone will be removed from the country.

A bond decision addresses custody during a case. The amount alone cannot establish the strength of an immigrant's claim to remain in the United States, and a court's median does not describe every person appearing there.

A 2026 Board of Immigration Appeals decision outlines additional factors judges may weigh, including a fixed U.S. address, length of residence, family connections, employment history and previous court appearances. Criminal history, immigration violations, attempts to flee authorities and manner of entry may also enter the assessment.

Those individual considerations limit what a comparison between cities can prove. Establishing why the medians diverge would require examining the circumstances behind the decisions, including the evidence presented and the population eligible for hearings.

Access to legal representation presents another uneven feature of the immigration court system. In a separate report published Sept. 15, TRAC found that only 24% of immigrants whose cases ended in removal orders in August had an attorney. That group included unaccompanied children.

Across completed immigration court cases, representation fell from 63% in fiscal 2021 to 32% in fiscal 2026 through August. Those figures cover immigration proceedings broadly and do not measure representation specifically at bond hearings.

The September report also identified large geographic differences in obtaining counsel. Among immigrants with new court cases filed during the preceding 90 days, 70.5% of Maine residents had representation, compared with 70.2% in Hawaii. West Virginia followed at 65.5%, Maryland at 59.1% and Massachusetts at 56.8%.

TRAC attributed the broader representation shortfall to demand outstripping available legal assistance. Unlike criminal defendants, immigrants in removal proceedings generally are not entitled to government-appointed counsel at public expense.

text:
The Supreme Court agreed Friday to review President Donald Trump’s ban on asylum at the southern border, a key part of his administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown.

What they're saying:

The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found the executive order banning asylum applications illegal. It's the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.

Federal law gives people the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.

RELATED: Trump admits immigration enforcement may have been too 'tough' in first interview since midterms

At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

The other side:

But immigration attorneys at the American Civil Liberties Union and National Immigrant Justice Center counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to unilaterally "eviscerate" legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

Big picture view:

The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn’t allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue.

The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

RELATED: Deportations not meeting Trump's aggressive targets, report finds

What's next:

The justices are expected to hear the case in the coming months and hand down a decision by the end of June.

It's the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings.

The justices decided another asylum case in favor of the administration earlier this year, clearing the way for the Trump administration to potentially revive a "metering" policy that has been used to turn back immigrants in years past.

title: ICE raids in Kansas meatpacking towns drove voters to the polls - 1News
description:
Here in Kansas, late September raids ignited a maelstrom of rage, turning many who had been apathetic, like Del Real, into determined voters.
The resistance came not only from Democrats or the Latino population, which has grown to about two-thirds of Dodge City.
But, from rural Kansas, immigration raids in places like Minneapolis and Chicago felt abstract.
Local Republican Chairman Scott Fischer, who describes himself as a supporter of strong borders, was surprised by the operation’s intensity.
More than half of Kansas voters in the Senate race disapprove of how ICE is handling its job, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.
text:
Jose Del Real looked over the crowd from the stage in a park, at hundreds of his neighbors with furious signs tucked under their arms, voicing their anger at immigration agents who had descended on their town and started rounding up their friends and family. His daughters, in the front row, were crying.

Del Real, an Army veteran who served two tours in Iraq, hadn’t voted in a decade. He thought it wouldn’t matter in this ruby red corner of Kansas. But the midterm election was weeks away.

He draped an American flag over his shoulders, put on his Iraq veteran cap and ended his speech with a message: “None of this matters if you do not vote. Let’s go vote.”

They did.

This county and two of its neighbours in southwestern Kansas, Republican strongholds where a steady stream of immigrants have settled over the decades to work at feed lots and slaughterhouses, swung wildly to the left.

The shift helped elect a Democratic US senator from Kansas for the first time in nearly a century, signaling the limits of President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation agenda.

Since Democrats won back control of Congress in a decisive rebuke to Republicans, Trump has sent mixed messages about how he plans to handle immigration enforcement going forward.

He suggested that his approach to deportations was too harsh but also named hard-liner Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff. Both parties will be recalibrating their approach ahead of the next presidential campaign.

Here in Kansas, late September raids ignited a maelstrom of rage, turning many who had been apathetic, like Del Real, into determined voters.

Masked officers in tactical gear banged on doors before dawn. They stopped cars in the middle of intersections. Businesses shuttered. Families feared leaving their houses. Children stopped going to school. Some livestreamed themselves being detained.

One man pleaded “God help me” in Spanish, his hands shaking, as he asked anyone watching to let his family know.

The resistance came not only from Democrats or the Latino population, which has grown to about two-thirds of Dodge City. Kansas' embattled Republican senator, Roger Marshall, who would lose his reelection bid to Adam Hamilton, issued a statement pleading with the administration to consult local officials before launching raids.

Del Real regrets he didn't vote in 2024, when Trump roared back into office pledging mass deportations.

“We had to see it in front of us,” Del Real said. “I had to see it in the flesh.”

The gates leading into Dodge City boast that it's the “Queen of the Cowtowns.”

Its main street is named after the classic Western set here, "Gunsmoke." Murals celebrating cowboy history mix with evidence of a changing culture: storefronts showcasing quinceañera dresses, Mexican bakeries, city signs printed in both Spanish and English.

Del Real’s family came from Mexico when he was a kindergartner. Like most here, they came to work.

The area — Dodge City and the region's other hubs, Garden City and Liberal — is known as the Golden Triangle of Meatpacking, responsible for about a quarter of the US beef supply.

Some here thought their importance to the nation’s food might spare them from the administration’s deportation campaigns, said Amy Soberanes, a 25-year-old local organizer.

Soberanes, the daughter of Mexican immigrants, said she and others tried for years to get people — particularly their young, Latino neighbors — engaged.

But, from rural Kansas, immigration raids in places like Minneapolis and Chicago felt abstract.

Then they saw their own streets in social media videos.

People were furious, said Soberanes, who worried the daily protests could get out of hand. They told people not to slash tires or break windows, to store up their anger and take it out on Election Day.

“We’ll see them at the ballot box,” she recalls repeating.

Her phone rang and rang. People she’d hassled to vote for years asked: How do I register?

“If ICE hadn’t come, we would still be red, 100%,” she said. “And so I thank Donald Trump for sending immigration here.”

No one knew immigration officers were coming.

Dodge City Commissioner Rick Sowers said he and other city officials found out just like everyone else, through social media or masses of unmarked trucks on their neighbors’ lawns.

They scrambled to get answers from the federal government – who they were looking for, who was in charge, how long they would stay – and never did.

The Trump administration issued statements naming five “heinous criminals” they said had been arrested.

But the Wichita Eagle dug into that claim and found none of those people were actually apprehended during the surge: Four had been deported months before and the fifth was already in prison, the newspaper found.

The agency said it detained 104 people from southwest Kansas.

Local officials have still never seen a list, Sowers said.

Local Republican Chairman Scott Fischer, who describes himself as a supporter of strong borders, was surprised by the operation’s intensity.

“There was a little showmanship,” he said. “I don’t know why it was like that.”

He said he still considers the county red — it voted, narrowly, for Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson.

The Associated Press called that race Thursday: Masterson lost to Democrat Cindy Holscher.

But some Dodge City Republicans abandoned the party in the US Senate race.

Dr. Russell Arben Fox, political science professor at Friends University in Wichita, said swings as dramatic as that one couldn't have happened without some white, moderate Republicans changing their minds.

More than half of Kansas voters in the Senate race disapprove of how ICE is handling its job, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.

That’s consistent with the 61% of voters who say this nationally.

Most of the Latino immigrants here are hard-working, family-oriented, faithful people – a perfect fit for conservative Kansas values, Fischer said, so local Republicans tend to have a nuanced view on immigration.

Some public officials have for years begged the federal government for reforms to provide a pathway for these workers who run the region’s economy.

“In general terms, mass deportation is not practical,” Fischer said. “When we say send them all home, what does that mean? Who is them?”

To many here, “them” this time meant relatives and friends. In this small town, nearly everybody is connected to everybody else, so they did what they could to help.

Oscar Soto delivered food to people afraid to leave home during the deportation raids.

He started calling it “the black week,” after the black plague. That’s what it felt like to him, a pestilence that arrived suddenly.

His mother came here from Mexico, he said, and though she is here legally, she was terrified.

“It seemed unreal,” he said. “It was stuff that’s never been seen here, and it was day after day after day.”

He works at a family-owned grocery, and strung a garland of flags from around the world above the counter when it opened.

Most customers are from Mexico and Guatemala, he said, but he wanted to signal that the store was for everyone.

Then he hung a big American flag from the ceiling. It means to him that anyone, from anywhere, can come here, work hard and build a life, free from fear.

That belief in the American dream was shaken for him when ICE arrived.

So he registered to vote for the first time at age 39.

He stood in line to cast his ballot, amazed by how many young, Latino voters were waiting along with him.

title: Beyond the Ballot: The U.S. Midterms and the Future of American Power
description:
Although the United States is now one of the world’s largest oil producers, it is not immune to the economic consequences of a war involving Iran.
And here comes the issue that I think has compounded an already structural problem within the United States having to do with decades-long redistribution from the bottom to the top,” Adly noted.
Another potential implication of the war is a shift in how U.S. partners view their security commitments with Washington.
El-Hadidy argued that foreign governments—including Russia, China, and countries of the European Union—understand that a shift in Congress wouldn’t necessarily translate to a shift in the current administration’s direction.
“My personal hunch is that it’s never going to return back to as it was before Trump,” El-Hadidy said.
text:
Since the Democratic Party’s electoral successes after November 3, incoming democratic lawmakers have been preparing investigations into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and they’re expected to challenge the administration’s military spending, particularly funding for the ongoing war in Iran.

However, analysts caution that congressional pressure does not directly translate to constraints on presidential authority, particularly given Trump’s veto powers and executive control over foreign policy.

Prior to the elections, the Center for American Studies and Research (CASAR) at the American University in Cairo (AUC) hosted a panel titled “US Midterm Elections: Expectations, Facts and Reality,” where speakers examined how the midterm elections could reshape the balance of power in Congress, constrain President Donald Trump’s administration, and influence the United States’ role both in the MENA region and globally.

The discussion extended beyond electoral predictions to consider a broader question: how much can an election actually change about the state of America?

“These elections have the potential to slow down some of the more extremist actions of the current American president,” said Mark Deets, an associate professor of African and world history and director of CASAR, who was also moderating the panel.

Domestic Repercussions for the United States

Sean Lee, assistant professor of political science at The American University in Cairo (AUC), argued that the United States is experiencing “democratic backsliding”, in which state institutions are abused to disadvantage political opponents.

Several factors that would work against the Republicans were identified by Lee, including the likelihood of lower turnout among Trump’s supporters in the midterms, the economic repercussions of the war in Iran, and corruption within the American political system.

These concerns would later feature prominently after the Democrats’ victory, as voters expressed frustration over the rising cost of living, the war, and the Trump administration’s handling of government affairs.

Lee considered the possibility of the Democrats winning to be “kind of a check on the presidency to some extent” while claiming that the United States can no longer be considered a democratic system, but rather an oligarchic or a competitive authoritarian system.

“They say that it’s a system where parties compete in meaningful elections, but incumbents systematically abuse state institutions to tilt the political playing field against their opponents,” Lee explained.

Lee pointed to gerrymandering as an example of how electoral arrangements can be utilized to disadvantage political opponents. By manipulating district boundaries, mapmakers can weaken a party’s electoral influence, either by splitting its voters across multiple districts or concentrating them in a few, limiting their ability to secure seats.

Although congressional redistricting typically takes place every ten years, current efforts have taken place at the behest of Donald Trump, beginning in Texas before spreading to other parts of the country.

Partisan gerrymandering in Tennessee and racial gerrymandering in Memphis were also cited by Lee. Nevertheless, he cautioned that the strategy could backfire in some states, potentially costing Republicans seats rather than helping them secure an advantage.

Moving from these structural attempts, he presented another aspect of a competitive authoritarian system, which is the “more acute weaponization of the U.S. government against political opponents”, where he mentioned the example of agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)––the investigative division of ICE—conducting a pre-dawn search at the home of U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar in Washington, D.C. Omar and democratic critics characterized the operation as political intimidation.

These instances, along with reported concerns that ICE agents could appear at polling stations, are part of efforts by the Republican incumbents to influence the election and “weaponize the government institutions against opponents”, Lee said. He said it fits the pattern of competitive authoritarianism, a concept developed by political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way. The data, he suggested, point the same way. Freedom House’s score had reached 93 percent in 2005 but declined to 81percent in 2025.

Concerns about ICE and DHS brought Lee’s discussion to a close, as he cited incidents involving “shooting citizens in the street and detaining people over their not only immigration status, but also in the case of Palestine protesters over their criticisms of, in this case, not even the United States, but of a foreign country, that is to say, Israel.”

Implications for Conflict in the Middle East

Beyond the question of American institutions, other panelists looked at what shifting power in Washington means for the world and especially the MENA region.

Amr Adly, an associate professor in the department of political science at AUC, argued that the relationship between the United States and the Middle East is not one-sided: just as American politics has shaped the region before, developments in the region have repeatedly reverberated through the global economy, including within the United States.

Using the examples of the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks, Adly illustrated how developments in the Middle East triggered major disruptions in global energy markets. Drawing a parallel between the Iranian Revolution, which contributed to the 1979 oil shock, and the current war involving Iran, he highlighted how geopolitical upheaval in the region can have consequences far beyond its borders. Although the United States is now one of the world’s largest oil producers, it is not immune to the economic consequences of a war involving Iran. The issue, however, extends beyond rising energy prices to who ultimately benefits from them.

“The distribution question, of course, is about who is getting the extra rent that is resulting from the higher energy prices. And here comes the issue that I think has compounded an already structural problem within the United States having to do with decades-long redistribution from the bottom to the top,” Adly noted.

The economic shift has a political counterpart, and in his view, the United States is increasingly acting in a “classical colonial role” in the Middle East, maintaining a direct military presence through fleets, troops, invasions, and bombing campaigns. The current war with Iran could expose the limits of American power if the United States fails to achieve its original objectives, particularly the removal of the Iranian regime, Adly argued, stating that the war is generating anxiety “within many imperialist circles within the United States elites”.

Another potential implication of the war is a shift in how U.S. partners view their security commitments with Washington. Adly argued that the war has exposed the vulnerabilities of existing security arrangements in the Gulf, potentially encouraging regional powers to reconsider their reliance on American security guarantees.

Pressure on those commitments is also building in Washington itself. He pointed to growing opposition to military intervention abroad among parts of both the political left and right, alongside deepening divisions over U.S.-Israel relations. Tracing this bipartisan resistance to the intervention in Iraq, he argued that the opposition to the U.S. dedicating resources “for such infrequent interventions” has been reflected in the votes and in public opinion.

“And that is yet another issue where the political class in general in the United States in both parties do not seem to be in line with what most of the Americans think,” Adly concluded.

Global Implications

Where Lee and Adly looked at the pressures on American power from within, Alaa El-Hadidy, a former ambassador to Turkey, Russia, and Romania, and now a professor of practice at AUC’s School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, looked at how other governments read it. He argued that foreign governments are following the midterms but don’t expect a shift in Congress to change Washington’s direction.

El-Hadidy argued that foreign governments—including Russia, China, and countries of the European Union—understand that a shift in Congress wouldn’t necessarily translate to a shift in the current administration’s direction. “So the address is not to go to Capitol Hill but to go to the White House,” he said.

El-Hadidy first pointed to the legislation targeting major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, which was signed into law on September 18, 2026. However, on October 16, Trump issued an executive order waiving the application of certain sanctions provisions under the law, an option that the legislation allowed, subject to reporting requirements.

Using this event as an example, El-Hadidy argued that it shows that Russia understands Trump’s transactional approach to politics and will continue to prioritize its relationship with the White House, rather than Congress, in pursuing its interests in Ukraine.

China, on the other hand, “is a little bit more sophisticated in their dealing with the Americans than Russians; the Chinese know how to play American internal politics more than Russia,” El-Hadidy argued. China was able to retaliate against Trump’s tariffs by imposing high tariffs on products produced by farmers—who are a constituency of Trump— thus pressuring Trump.

Because bilateral trade decisions can be highly affected by Congress, El-Hadidy noted that China would definitely be more interested in the midterm election results in comparison to Russia. He added that this might be because China does not have the same stakes as Russia—no war on its border—but only the question of Taiwan, which Trump had publicly said he’s using as a “good negotiating chip”.

However, El Hadidy believes that the EU has more at stake in the midterms than Russia or China, particularly because of security, NATO, and trade relations.

“The EU, like the Chinese and the Russians, understands quite well where the power of the Congress really is, where the role of the Congress [in] American foreign policy really is, and who has the real power, especially under this current administration,” El-Hadidy stated.

Has the Name of the Game Changed?

El-Hadidy’s remarks highlighted the concentration of executive power under Trump, raising a broader question in light of the Democrats’ electoral gains: was this concentration of power specific to the Trump administration, or does it reflect a more lasting transformation of the American political system?

“My personal hunch is that it’s never going to return back to as it was before Trump,” El-Hadidy said. “What Trump has done in the long run, is that he has given the presidency such new tools, which were in the Constitution, but were hidden or people or scholars did not pay enough attention to. This is going to be a very dangerous tool to use by whoever becomes president.”

REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES

Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital voters who split their tickets between Trump and down-ballot Democrats in 2024 were responding this year to both affordability pressures and the president’s immigration crackdown.

"He made a promise that he was going to bring prices down on day one. Liberation didn't happen, so people remembered that," Cuellar, whose district encompasses border town Laredo, told Fox News Digital.

"Second thing is he said he was going to focus on criminals. He didn't stop there. He started going after construction workers."

Democrats’ wins came as an estimated 14.5 million Latinos voted across the country in the 2026 midterms, according to UnidosUS. The group’s Texas state director, Eric Holguín, said Democratic support among Latino voters rivaled levels seen in 2008, when Barack Obama won the presidency.
